paragraphs.text: Eusebius sends greetings in the Lord to his most honoured and beloved fellow minister Flacillus.

You should not be surprised that a brief reply from me has been enough to answer Marcellus's long-winded and wordy writing. Few words are needed to overturn views that even ordinary people condemn at first sight. That is why, in my first two books, I simply set out the man's own words. I offered no rebuttal at all, and his words themselves made the case against them plain. Now I have gone beyond that exposure and refuted those same views in the three books before you. He composed one single treatise, enormous and full of wandering. He says he did this because he acknowledges one God, so that dividing his writing into parts would not somehow lead him, without his noticing, to give the Son of God room to subsist as a distinct being. We, however, honour the all-holy and thrice-blessed Trinity, so we have covered the whole subject in a matching number of books. We have avoided wordiness and set out the true theology concisely and briefly. Whether what I have written is sufficient you may judge for yourself as you read it. If anything is lacking, you can supply that as well, as a brother makes up a brother's shortcomings and heals them by correction wherever they need treatment.
I pray that you may be well and may always remember me before the Lord.

I had thought that the quotations of Marcellus's own words, which I gathered in the preceding books, were enough to refute themselves. They contained so open and blatant a denial of the Son of God that the people nurtured by the church of God would shun their teaching even without any rebuttal.

On further reflection, however, I became concerned that some might be drawn away from the church's theology by the many passages the man cites in support of what he thought would help his case. So I decided that I must now also expose the falsehood of these. Then everyone may learn that not a single passage of the inspired Scripture bore witness in agreement with him as he denied the Son of God. Every one of them plainly said the opposite, and they straightforwardly correct his mistaken interpretations of the divine Scriptures. Alongside this exposure I will also present the theology of our Saviour. I have nothing new to say and no clever discovery of my own. I am putting forward the uncorrupted teaching of the church of God, which she received from the beginning from those who were eyewitnesses and hearers of the Word, and which she keeps safe.

Before examining these passages, I must deal with something else. In the middle of his treatise I found him attacking Sabellius, and I was astonished at the man's foolishness. He did not hesitate to speak ill of the very person he should have praised above all others, since Sabellius shared his opinion and his mind. I did not think I should pass this over in silence, so I will include a refutation of it in the present work as well. His slander of God's ministers brought blame on himself and good repute on those who were set free from communion with him,

yet it had some plausibility, since he seemed to be disparaging those who were not his friends. But to strike at himself without noticing it, by reviling someone who shares his mind, seems to me both shameless and senseless. That this is so, he himself proves. Like Sabellius he introduces God as a 'Son-Father', if not in plain words, then at least in fact. He does away with the Son's distinct existence and defines God as one, and he calls this one God his own Father and in turn his own Son. For he grants that the Word is the Word within God,

and defines him as one and the same with God. He then says that God is called the Word's Father, and that the Word is his Son. But the Word is not truly a Son, existing as a distinct being. He is properly and truly a Word. Indeed, Marcellus stresses that he is a Word not in a loose sense, but properly and truly a Word, and nothing other than a Word.

But if he is nothing other than a Word, he was clearly not properly and truly a Son either. He was called Son only loosely, in sound and in name. And by saying that the Word is one and the same with God, Marcellus declared that the one who became flesh and was born of the virgin was God himself. The church of God rejected this very doctrine long, long ago, when Sabellius uttered it, and counted him among the godless heretics.

The children of the Jews were the first to receive the confession of one God, as opposed to the polytheistic error of the Greeks. But the saving grace of God has given the church a special privilege: to know this same God also as Father of an only-begotten Son. The church knows Jesus Christ alone as Son, and no one else. He is not Son by the birth of the flesh he took on, for she has been taught to call that 'the form of a servant' and 'Son of Man'. He is Son by his birth from God the Father himself before all ages, a birth unknown to all. By this birth the fullness of the Father's Godhead established him as Son and also as God. His Godhead is not his own possession, separated from the Father. It is not an unoriginate and unbegotten Godhead, nor one drawn from some other source, foreign and alien to the Father. He is filled from the Father's very being, which pours out on him as from a spring. For the great apostle taught that in him alone the whole fullness of the Father's Godhead dwells. Therefore the church of God proclaims one God, and there is no other besides him. She also proclaims one only-begotten Son of God, the image of the Father's Godhead, and for that reason God.

Most people could not grasp this theology, and so they devised various paths of error. (1) Some granted that the Son was God but denied the human being he had taken on. (2) Others supposed him a mere man and did not recognize the God in him. (3) Still others, afraid of seeming to introduce a second God, defined the Father and the Son as one and the same. The church of God turns away from them and takes pride in the gospel proclamation of the truth. She boasts that she has one God who is over all, and she claims as her own one only-begotten Son, God from God, Jesus Christ. She confesses that this same one, her Saviour, also became Son of Man. He was Son of God even before he became man, and he also became what he was not, because of the Father's unspeakably great love for humankind.

This is what the word of truth cries out in the person of the church. But those who deny the Son of God and say that God is one and nothing else, why do they trouble the church for nothing, when they ought to join the synagogues of the Jews? And why do they entangle themselves in blasphemous statements and slander the one God with a double title, if they suppose that the same one is Father and also Son? Whose Father is he, if no Son exists? And whose Son will he be, if the one who begot him does not exist before him? If there is only one, then he himself must be the one who became flesh, suffered, and lived out a mortal life among human beings.

When Sabellius said these things, the church of God drove him far away, for he dared to utter godless and impious doctrines. Now Marcellus is trying to revive them, using an unconvincing argument as a screen. He rightly defines God as one, but he says that this God has a Word within himself, united and joined to him. Then he calls one part of the one God 'Father' and the other 'Son', as though there were a double and composite being in him.

If one must choose between evils, Sabellius is far better than Marcellus. He does not divide the unoriginate, unbegotten, and divine power, but plainly confesses that Father and Son are the same. And the Jew is far better than both. He does not divide the one God into Father and Son as Marcellus does, nor does he introduce the same one as 'Son-Father' as Sabellius does. He worships God, and he acknowledges and awaits God's Christ, whose coming was proclaimed through the prophets. Yet because they did not receive him when he came, they have paid the penalty for their unbelief in him and will pay it still.

But those who long to believe in the one who has come will acknowledge these three: the one born of the seed of David and of that same holy virgin; the Son of God who dwelt in him, who existed beforehand and subsists as a real being; and God his Father, by whom he constantly confesses that he was sent. For us, then, as the apostle says, there is 'one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things'. He is the pre-existent only-begotten Son of God. Third is the one who is Son of Man according to the flesh, whom the Son of God took on for our sake.

But the body he took on was not the same as the Son of God who took it on. Nor could the Son of God himself be thought one and the same as the one who begot him. Since these three are given, those who accept two and do away with the third should be cast out of the church.

Some godless heretics rejected the Saviour's flesh and said that he appeared on earth only as a kind of apparition. They were the first to miss the mark of the truth. Others accepted the dispensation in the flesh but denied the pre-existent Son of God, and, as I said, they devised for themselves various wrong roads. Some said he was a mere man, sharing the nature common to all and superior in nothing except the excellence of his virtue. Others taught that the God of the universe himself dwelt in the body, and that he was called his own Son because of the dispensation he underwent as a man. These grant two, God and man, but deprive themselves of the third, for they deny the Saviour himself, the only-begotten Son of God.

Long ago Sabellius, and now Marcellus, were carried away by the views of these people. Like the unbelieving Jews, they insisted that they knew very well the God who is over all. They also agreed on the second, the flesh born of the holy virgin. But they pushed aside the third, the very heart of the salvation of us all, the Son of God, who is light and truth. In denying the Son they also fell away from the light of the truth.

So you will hear them confess one God and honour the Saviour's flesh. As for the Son of God who dwelt in the flesh, they accept him with their voice and lips but reject him in fact. For they should have looked for a Son of God who truly lives and subsists, who is neither the same as the body he took on nor the same as God the Father. No one could speak piously by calling the God who is beyond the universe a Son, for whose Son could he be who is clothed with the unoriginate and unbegotten Godhead? Nor will anyone who says that the only-begotten Son of God is himself the Father escape the punishment that awaits blasphemers.

Therefore the church of God, keeping a straight course along the direct, royal road, has rejected all the other byways. She hands down to her nurslings the knowledge of the divine grace. In the very mystery of rebirth she teaches them to confess their faith 'in one God, the Father Almighty'. In this way she enables them to know a theology that is perfect, precise, and complete. It hands down one God, and so separates itself from the polytheistic error of the Greeks. It knows him as Father, and so parts ways with the teaching of the Jews. It confesses him as Almighty, and so turns away from the impiety of the godless heretics.

No heretic, at any rate, would say that the Father of Christ is himself God the Almighty. Likewise no Jew would confess that God is Father, since he does not know the only-begotten Son, and no Greek would say that he knows only one God. Therefore the church cleanses away the error of all these and proclaims the one God. She teaches that he is both Father and Almighty: Father of Christ alone, and God, Creator, and Lord of all the rest. In the same way she hands down Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all ages. He is not the same as the Father. He exists and lives in his own right, and he is with the Father as a true Son: God from God, Light from Light, Life from Life. He was begotten of the Father for the salvation of the universe, in ways that are unutterable and inexpressible, wholly unknown to us and beyond our grasp. He did not come into being like other begotten things, nor does he live a life like that of the beings that came into being through him. He alone was brought forth from the Father himself, and he is Life itself.

It was fitting for the God who is over all to put forth this only-begotten offspring before every created thing and before all ages. He was to be a kind of base and unbreakable foundation for the things that would come into being through him. That is why, before all that was to be, God begot the Son as a ray of light, a spring of life, and a treasury of good things. In him, as the divine apostle says, 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge'.

The Father, who alone is good, established the Son as the source of all these great goods. He is Life itself, giving life to the universe. He is the true Light itself, enlightening every intelligent and rational being. He is the Word itself and Wisdom itself, who brings all things into being and governs them wisely and rationally. For these reasons he alone, and no one else, is called and is the only-begotten Son of God.

So one may rightly find fault with those who have dared to call him a creature, made out of nothing like the other creatures. How can he still be a Son? And how can he be God's only-begotten if he is assigned the same nature as the other creatures? In that case he would be their brother rather than the Son of God. He would be one of the many things that have come into being, since he would share with them in creation out of nothing.

But that is not what the divine oracles teach about him. When they teach how created things came to exist, they testify that all things without exception came into being through him. As the apostolic teachings say: 'All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being'; and 'In him all things in heaven and on earth were created, things visible and invisible... all things have been created through him and for him; and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.'

But when they set out the theology concerning him, they separate him from all other things. They know him as Lord, Master, Maker, God, and Saviour of the universe. They declare that he alone, and no one else, is the only-begotten Son of God. They call him alone Wisdom, Word, Life, and Light, 'the image of the invisible God' and 'the radiance of eternal light'. And they teach us to believe countless other things like these about him. In these ways they show the special relation of the Father's Godhead to him alone, as to an only-begotten Son.

That is why, at the streams of the Jordan, the Father's voice proclaimed him alone as beloved Son, bearing witness with a great cry: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' And at the transfiguration on the mountain the voice repeated its testimony and confirmed the same word.

The God of the universe himself has given him this testimony. The evangelist expressly teaches that he is the only-begotten Son when he says: 'No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son (or: the only-begotten God), who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.' And the Saviour himself confirmed this in his teaching about himself, when he said: 'For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life.'

After these words, anyone who defines the Son as a thing made out of nothing, a creature brought forth from non-being, gives him only the name without realizing it, while denying that he is truly a Son. For one who came into being out of nothing could not truly be the Son of God, any more than any other begotten thing could.

But the one who is truly the Son of God, brought forth from him as from a father, would rightly be called the only-begotten and beloved of the Father. In this way he would also be God. For what could God's offspring be, if not something made like the one who begot it? A king builds a city but does not beget a city. He is said to beget a son, not to build one. A craftsman is the maker, not the father, of what he makes, and he would not be called the maker of a son born of him. So too the God of the universe would rightly be called Father of the Son, but Creator and Maker of the world.

If someone finds it said once in Scripture, 'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works', he must look into the meaning of the passage, which I will set out a little later. He must not, like Marcellus, unsettle the church's most fundamental doctrine on the strength of a single word. For Marcellus too, having heard once that the Son is the Word, fell into the notion of a human word and denied the Son's existence.

Both the Son himself and the Father testify that he is Son. How then can it be right to compare him with other created things? How will he be only-begotten if he is counted among the multitude of things that have come into being? His very title of Son shows his natural relation to the Father, and the name 'only-begotten' in turn touches on his kind, on his birth itself, and on his being the only one, with no one else sharing his sonship. But these people seem to have suffered the same affliction as Marcellus.

Marcellus, afraid of speaking of two gods, put forward the denial of the Son and rejected his distinct existence. These others grant two beings, one unbegotten and the other created out of nothing, and so hold that there is one God. But for them the Son will no longer be the only-begotten, nor Lord, nor God. He will have no share in the Father's Godhead and will be compared with the other creatures, inasmuch as he came to exist out of nothing. But the church does not teach this way.

She proclaims the Son of God as God and Lord, and teaches that he is truly Son and God. He is not like the many who are called sons and gods only as a title, of whom it is said: 'I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.' He alone, begotten of the Father himself, 'was in the form of God', and was 'the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation'. That is why the church has learned to honour, revere, and worship him alone as her Lord, Saviour, and God.

If these people are afraid that they might seem to proclaim two gods, let them know this. Even though we confess the Son as God, there would be only one God: the one who alone is unoriginate and unbegotten, who possesses Godhead as his own, and who is the cause of the Son's existence and of his being what he is. The Son himself confesses that he lives because of him, when he says plainly: 'Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father', and 'For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.'

That is why he teaches that the Father is both our God and his own, when he says: 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.' And the great apostle teaches that God is the head of the Son himself, while the Son is the head of the church. In one place he says: 'And the head of Christ is God'; in another he says of the Son: 'And he gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body.'

So the Son is the leader and head of the church, and the Father is his head. In this way there is one God, the Father of the only-begotten Son, and one head of Christ himself. Since there is one source and one head, how could there be two gods? There is only that one God, who claims no one higher than himself and no other cause of himself. He possesses Godhead as his own, unoriginate and unbegotten, the Godhead of monarchical authority, and has shared his own Godhead and life with the Son. It is he who established all things through the Son, who sends him, who gives him orders, who commands him, who teaches him, who hands over all things to him. He glorifies him, exalts him above all, and has shown him to be king of the universe. He hands over all judgement to him and wills that we too obey him. He bids him occupy the throne at the right hand of his majesty, addressing him and saying:

'Sit at my right hand.' Because of all this he is the God of the Son himself as well. In obedience to him his only-begotten Child 'emptied himself', 'humbled himself', took on 'the form of a servant', and 'became obedient to the point of death'. To him the Son also prays, him he obeys when he commands, to him he gives thanks. He teaches us to regard the Father alone as the true God, and confesses that the Father is greater than himself. Above all this, he wants all of us to know that the Father is his own God.

Since the Son glorifies his own Father in this way, the Father glorifies him in return and has shown him to be Lord, Saviour, and God of the universe, sharing the throne of his kingdom. The church of God has been taught these things. So she rightly knows him as her own God, Lord, and Saviour, and as the only-begotten Son of the God who is over all. She refuses to call any other created being God, and knows this one alone as God, the only one whom the Father begot from himself,

as he himself declared through Solomon when he said: 'Before the mountains were established, and before all the hills, he begets me.' In this saying he hints at the divine powers above the world by the mountains and hills.

Suppose someone pries into how God could beget, and how the one who is beyond all things can be a Father. The boldness of the question is silenced by the one who said: "Do not seek what is too deep for you, and do not examine what is too high for you. Think about what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things." Paul too said, "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!" Let him persuade anyone who dares to go further not to attempt what cannot be reached. Otherwise, let that person first tell us how the things he says came into being from what was not came to exist, and in what manner, when before they did not exist at all in any way.

For God did not make the universe with his hands like our craftsmen do, taking matter that already existed. It is impossible by nature for human beings to bring what does not exist at all out of non-being into being, yet this was possible for him. He became the maker of all things not as a human does but in ways we cannot speak of or express. In the same way, and much more so, the begetting of his only-begotten would be unsearchable and untraceable. This is true not, as one might say, for us alone, but also for all the powers higher than us.

Things far lower in nature, set beneath the unspeakable divine essence and very far from it, could never reach an understanding of what lies beyond and above. Things that did not exist before, but were brought by him from non-being into being, could never know the first generation of the one who brought them forth and caused them to exist. Shall we, then, safely inquire into unspeakable things and busy ourselves with how the Father begot the Son? We are creatures of yesterday, clothed in skin and flesh, strung together with bones and sinews, and we do not even understand our own affairs. That countless things right at our feet escape our knowledge will be clear from what follows.

For who could say how the soul is shut up in the body, how it leaves, or how it was put there in the first place? What is its form, its shape, its appearance, its essence? I will not yet go into prying questions about demons, or the essence of angels, or principalities and thrones and dominions, or authorities and world-rulers.

If we are at a loss in all these matters, why must we search out knowledge of the Godhead that has no beginning and is unbegotten? Why ask about what cannot be reached, namely how God came to be Father of an only-begotten Son? It is as if the Father's voice were not enough for us as testimony to the Beloved. He proclaimed him, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him."

Since he commands us to listen to him, let us obey the royal law and listen to the beloved Son. He will show what he wants us to know about himself when he says: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life." We must therefore believe in him in order to obtain eternal life. For "whoever believes in him," he says, "has eternal life."

He does not say "whoever knows how he was begotten of the Father." If that were required, no one would have any share in eternal life, since it has been said that "no one has known the Father except the Son, and no one has known the Son except the Father alone who begot him." Faith, then, is enough for our salvation. It allows us to know God the Father Almighty and to acknowledge his only-begotten Son as Savior. Among other things, the Son also taught this: "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit." And "God is spirit."

It follows that what is begotten of God must be God. The God who is beyond all things is utterly foreign and separate in nature from earthly flesh. To the same degree, we must understand that the way the Father begot the Son is foreign to the way fleshly beings come into being. He brought him into existence without emitting anything, without changing, without being moved by passion, and without undergoing anything at all of what we know from our own experience.

For he was not a body, so we cannot attribute to him any outflow, lessening, extension, alteration, change, flowing, part, or passion. Apart from all these, he brought about the generation in a way we cannot speak of or reckon. Indeed, no created nature at all can search it out or trace it. The sun, too, begets its radiance, and the Son is called "the radiance of eternal light" and "the radiance of glory." Yet this is not after the image of light that the senses perceive. Beyond every comparison, he brought the Son into existence in ways that cannot be spoken or grasped, and he is one and only-begotten.

Let every mouth be stopped of the impious and godless men who are sick with the error of many gods. They dragged down the unique and singular generation of the only-begotten Son into a multitude and proclaimed a "father of men and gods." In doing so they mixed men with gods and made the same father share their nature. These men uttered this impious and godless phrase through the working of demons. They imagined gods of the same nature and the same passions as the mortal, passion-prone, and sinful human race, along with a common father of these gods who must surely resemble his children. The herald of the Church, however, proclaims to all one only-begotten Son of the one God. God brought him into existence for the salvation and providential care of all created things.

Created nature is varied: some beings have bodies and some do not, some have souls and some do not, some are rational and some not, some mortal and some immortal. Because it falls so far short of what is higher, this nature could not draw near to the God who is above all and over all, nor share in the flashing radiance of his divinity. Through the weakness of its nature it would have slipped far, very far away, had it not obtained God the Savior as its helper. Fittingly, then, the Father's love for humankind set his only-begotten Child over all things, to pass through all things, to preside over all, and to water them with the bounty that comes from him.

The Father who begot him appointed him alone as shepherd and savior, guardian and protector, physician and helmsman of all things together, both in heaven and on earth. He placed in his hands alone the rudder that holds the universe together and governs it. The Son himself teaches this when he says, "All things have been handed over to me by my Father," and again, "For the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."

He received this charge from the Father like a wise helmsman. Standing over the whole world and looking up to his Father, he steers and guides the universe with his hand on the rudder. He does not overlook even the least of those who need what he provides, nor does he disdain the smallest. That is why he is present to all, giving each what is fitting. Like a physician tending the whole of creation, he supplies what is suited to its salvation.

So it is fitting that he did not disdain human life either. Long before, he gave his help to the God-loving men of every age. At one time he appeared in human form to the forefathers of the Hebrews. At another he laid down suitable laws for their descendants. To those who came later he gave oracles through the prophets about his coming divine appearance, which was to shine on all humankind.

When the time of these things had passed, he fulfilled the ancient oracles in deeds. At last he came in person and mingled and lived among mortal life. He, the only-begotten Son of God himself, used the body as his instrument, as if dwelling in a divine statue. Through it he spoke with the human race in teachings, in healings, and in the secret lessons of divine wisdom.

By the Father's will and out of surpassing love for humankind, he went for their sake even as far as the gates of death. He did this so that he might count those here below worthy of his grace as well and draw them up to the life that is with him. Thus "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself." He endured the plan of salvation in the flesh, though he existed before it and was honored with the divinity of the Father's glory. Yet "he did not regard being equal with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient" to the Father "to the point of death." Death had gained mastery over the whole race through the one man who sinned. In the same way, eternal life was now to reign through his grace over those who believe in him and through him come to know his God and Father.

It was right, then, that the Church, proclaiming these things, rejected Sabellius. He had counterfeited a false coin, the denial of the Son of God, even though he said, much like Marcellus, that he knew one God and that there was none besides him. Likewise, the first heralds of our Savior himself called certain people "Ebionites," a Hebrew word meaning "poor in understanding." These people said they knew one God and did not deny the Savior's body, but did not know the divinity of the Son.

Then there was the man from Samosata. He taught that Jesus was the Christ of God, and like Marcellus he confessed one God over all. Even so, the fathers of the Church declared him a stranger to the Church of God, because he did not confess that Christ was both Son of God and God before his birth in the flesh. He was driven far from the Church as one who had sinned impiously against Christ.

Sabellius, as one who offended against the Father himself, whom he dared to call the Son, suffered the same punishment as the godless heretics. Marcellus, suspecting he would suffer the same, devised a newer contrivance for his error. He defined God and the Word within him as one, while granting him two titles, Father and Son. Yet he did not go unnoticed or get away, but was at last caught in his own nets.
Even before he was caught, however, he was stricken in conscience and set about reviling Sabellius to shake off suspicion.

Hear how he slandered the man, naming him outright and writing about him in these very words: "For Sabellius too slipped from the right faith and knew neither God nor his holy Word accurately. Whoever does not know the Word is ignorant of the Father as well. 'For no one knows the Father,' he says, 'except the Son,' that is, the Word. It is through himself that the Word gives knowledge of the Father. So he also spoke to those Jews of that time who thought they knew God but rejected his Word, through whom alone God is known: 'No one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son reveals him.' Since it was impossible to know God any other way, he teaches people to know him through his own Word. So Sabellius too went astray, since he did not know the Father and his Word accurately."

This is what Marcellus wrote, clearing himself of the suspicion of Sabellianism, at least in words and speech. In his thinking, however, and in his agreement with the man, he is caught and pierced by the same arrows. For my part, I would have prayed that he not fall into the same errors. As it is, he plainly offends worse than Sabellius did. Sabellius perhaps erred through ignorance. Marcellus, however, admits that the man erred and then hurls himself over the obvious cliff of the same impiety, so he deserves no pardon at all. But let us examine what he has said.

First, he said that neither Sabellius nor the Jews knew God because they did not know the Word. We must therefore consider what kind of Word he has in mind. If he means the only-begotten Son of God, who subsists and lives, then he himself did not know him either. Our Savior spoke of the Son in many ways. He often called himself the only-begotten Son and never called himself the Word, and throughout all the Gospels he taught that he was the Son of God. For this reason he even calls Peter blessed for saying, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," and testifies that this knowledge came to him by the Father's revelation: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven." Yet this admirable man writes these words, word for word, as though his ears were stopped up: "And for this reason he does not call himself Son of God, but everywhere calls himself Son of Man, so that by such a confession he may prepare man to become son of God by adoption, through communion with him."

You see how he does not dare to confess him as Son of God, so as not to abandon the doctrine of Sabellius. Instead he calls him Son of Man because of the flesh he took on. Throughout his own treatise he calls him the Word, constantly stressing that he was nothing other than the Word.
Even where he criticizes Sabellius, he cites the Savior's words: "No one has known the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son reveals him."

Then, as if correcting those words, he again puts "Word" in place of "Son." He says, "'For no one knows the Father,' he says, 'except the Son,' that is, the Word." He continues, "For it is through himself that the Word gives knowledge of the Father," and adds, "It was impossible to know God any other way than through his own Word." Once again he puts "Word" in place of "Son" and calls him "his own Word." In so few words he mentions the Word many times but the Son not even once. He even alters the Savior's own saying,

inserting "that is, the Word" in place of "the Son," as though "Son" were not the better match for the title "Father." It was right and natural for the Savior to pair "Son" with "Father." This man, however, refuses to say "Son" and harps on "Word" over and over. He accuses Sabellius of denying the Son, yet he does the same thing himself and puts on a show, thinking that by slandering Sabellius he can deflect the suspicion of false belief. If he blames Sabellius for denying the Son of God, he ought to have blamed himself first. But if he blames him for not knowing the Word as Marcellus himself defined it, the charge was unjust.

Marcellus says there is a Word in God through whom God spoke to Moses and the prophets. Neither Sabellius nor even the Jews who deny the Christ of God were ignorant of this Word. Indeed, anyone at all, not only among the Jews but also among the Greeks, would say he knows this Word perfectly well. For who would not confess that God has reason, just as he is wise and good and powerful? Sabellius would not deny that he knows this. But he did not confess a Son of God who is living and subsisting, who exists and existed before the flesh. Because of this agreement with Marcellus, he was driven out of the Church of God just as Marcellus was.
It is clear that Marcellus held the same views as Sabellius, for he declared that God and his Word are one and the same. At times he says in these very words:

"If the inquiry concerned the spirit alone, the Word would reasonably appear to be one and the same as God." At other times he compares the Word of God to the human word and says that the word within a man is one and the same as the man and is separated from him by nothing except the activity of acting. This is why at times he declared that before the world was formed nothing existed except God. Again he said in these very words, "When the world had not yet come into being, there was nothing other than God alone."

At other times he compared the Word of God to our word that signifies meaning, writing as follows: "Just as all things that have come into being came into being from the Father through the Word, so too the things the Father speaks are signified through the Word." Having called him a signifying word in these lines, he goes on to present him as inseparable in hypostasis and one and the same as the Father. He says something like this: "This, I think, is easy for sensible people to understand even from a small and humble example drawn from ourselves."

"For no one can separate a man's word from him in power and hypostasis. The word is one and the same as the man and is separated from him by nothing except the activity of acting." Again he uses the same image where he says: "For everything the Father says, he is seen everywhere to say through the Word. This is clear from ourselves as well, so far as small things may be compared to great and divine ones. For we too do everything we wish to say and do, as far as we can, by our own word."

These words should be heard as coming no more from Marcellus than from Sabellius. The only difference might be that Marcellus is mocking Sabellius because Sabellius did not dare to shamelessly call the signifying word in God, as Marcellus conceives it, "Son." For Sabellius was not, after all, so senseless as to grant God over all a word in the same way men have one, nor so foolish as to call a word that has no subsistence the Son of God. Therefore Sabellius, saying there is one God and denying the Son,

said that the same one was Father and Son, which followed from the premise he had set himself. Marcellus, like him, grants that God and the Word within him are one and the same. He idly admits that Sabellius erred, but not that he himself did too.

He ought either to have accepted Sabellius as well, or to have blamed himself too and, while blaming Sabellius, to have turned away from the false belief they shared. He should not have pictured God like a sculptor, talking with his own thought and his own reasoning and urging himself on: "Come, let us make, come, let us fashion a statue." For that, he said, is how God too spoke the words "Let us make man."

Nor should he have posited in God at one time an inner word, as in a man, and at another a signifying word, like the word we speak aloud. Such things would be more tolerable to hear from Sabellius, or from one of the Jews who openly deny the Son of God, than from a Christian.

But he, as though priding himself on Jewish teaching, brings into the Church of Christ this impious and godless doctrine that the Son of God does not exist. Throughout the whole treatise he labored over, he argues that before the world came into being nothing existed except God alone, so as to shut the Son out. He even exalts himself, boasting that he knows one God,

as though we did not say this too. We have accepted that the Son of God is truly Son, and we have learned from him to acknowledge one God, who is at once God and Father of the only-begotten Son. The Son is plainly his own true Son, begotten of him before all ages. Before taking on flesh he was called not only the Word, as this noble fellow lays down, but countless other names besides. Yet here too Marcellus misrepresents divine Scripture, insisting that before his coming in the flesh he was called nothing other than the Word.

Hear, then, how he asserts this, writing in these very words: "So it is clear from every side that no other name suits the eternity of the Word except the one spoken by John, the most holy disciple and apostle of God, at the beginning of the Gospel. After taking on flesh he is proclaimed Christ and Jesus, Life and Way and Day and Resurrection and Door and Bread, and whatever else the divine Scriptures may call him. But we must not on that account be ignorant of the first name, namely that he was the Word. This is why the most holy evangelist and disciple of the Lord, keenly awake in the Spirit, recalled the beginning from above and nothing more recent. He said, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,' to show that any new and more recent name came to him from his new and recent plan of salvation in the flesh."

Next he adds: "So before he came down and was born through the Virgin, he was only the Word. What else was it, before taking on human flesh, that came down 'in the last days,' as he himself also wrote, and was born of the holy Virgin? Nothing other than the Word." And again he continues: "For before, as I have often said, he was nothing other than the Word."

He adds again: "For the Word 'was in the beginning,' being nothing other than the Word. But the man united to the Word, who did not exist before, became man, as John teaches us: 'And the Word became flesh.' This is why he clearly mentions the Word alone."

"Whether divine Scripture mentions the name Jesus or the name Christ, it clearly names the Word of God as he is after taking on human flesh. If anyone claims he can show the name Christ or Jesus applied to the Word alone even before the New Covenant, he will find that it was said prophetically." After some other remarks he goes on: "Fittingly, then, before the descent he was what we have often said, the Word. After the descent and the taking on of flesh, he also received various titles." These are the passages that convict Marcellus of denying the Son of God, who exists and lives and is truly Son, and of introducing a bare word.

The statements of his quoted earlier have also shown what kind of word he supposed him to be. He used the human word as an example and said that the Word is one and the same as God. Having laid this down as his starting point, he went on, in keeping with the premise he had set himself, to misrepresent divinely inspired Scripture and to twist its meaning.

For now it seemed right to me to examine a few of these points briefly. I also wanted to show those who do not know that no scripture agrees with him in his innovations and his departure from the sound faith. On the contrary, all of scripture speaks against the accounts he has wrongly adopted and testifies against them. This needed to be shown above all to those who honor the man, so that none of them, through their own inexperience of the divine readings, should suppose that he has hit the mark of the truth.

The first point to examine is the one he first dared to declare: that before the Son of God was born through the virgin, he was called by no other name than "Word." For he claims that before the coming in the flesh he was nothing other than Word, and that he was not named otherwise, except prophetically. He says that he both was and was named Word and nothing else, and that only after the coming in the flesh did he receive his various titles.
So this must be shown first: that he made this declaration ignorantly, without knowledge of the divine scriptures.
1. For first of all the divine evangelist John himself, who did call him Word,

2. not long after but immediately, in the very next breath, named him God, saying, "and the Word was God." He could have said, "and the Word was God's," but he did not say this, so that no one might claim he was like the word found among human beings. Instead he calls him God, and in this way shows the surpassing greatness of the divine dignity that belongs to him.
3. Then, passing on to another aspect of his praise, he named him Light, and by this very name showed that he existed before he took up the body,

where he says of the Baptist, "He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light, which enlightens every person coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him."

You see how in these words he named him not only Word, as Marcellus thought, but also God and Light, and taught both that he pre-existed and that the world came into being through him. For just as he had said earlier that all things came into being through God the Word and that without him nothing came into being, so he says the same of the Light: "for the world," he says, "came into being through him."

So the Light and God the Word are one and the same. And in saying that through him came into being now "the world," now "all things," he presents him in his role as God's servant. The evangelist could have said, "all things came into being by him," and again, "and the world came into being by him," yet he did not say "by him" but "through him," in order to direct us back to the Father's own authority as maker of the universe.

Moreover, he says, "the world did not know him." Yet all human beings acknowledge the God who is over all through their natural notions, and the children of the Jews foremost of all, led by the hand by the prophetic scriptures, as Marcellus himself acknowledges further on.

So the one whom "the world did not know" was someone else: God and Word, who both was and was named Light. But this was not a light perceived by the senses, nor one that illuminates the eyes of the flesh as the sun does, for then the nature of irrational animals too would have shared in it. As it is, he teaches what kind of light it was when he says, "It was the light that enlightens every person coming into the world." This rational light, then, belonged to human beings alone.

That is why, by an intellectual and rational power, he made the souls created after his image and likeness intellectual and rational. And just as he was not a light perceived by the senses, neither was he the one who is beyond all things, God himself. For "God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all." The one, indeed, was unapproachable light, as the divine apostle teaches when he says, "dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see."

But the other "was in the world," enlightening "every person coming into the world." And, he says, the world too came into being through this light; that is, the greater one, the Father, constituted the universe through the Son. These, then, are three auspicious and reverent titles of the powers of the Son of God, which the theologian adopted together as he began his writing: Word, God, and Light.

4. Then the same writer adds a fourth, calling the same one Only-begotten, where he says, "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." So he also bore the title Only-begotten of God before he took on flesh. For, he says, even though "the Word became flesh" for our sake, nevertheless we to whom he deigned to show his own divinity did not look at the flesh (for this was "the form of a slave"), but at his glory, which was contemplated apart from the body with a pure mind. "We beheld his glory," a glory beyond words and surpassing all mortal reasoning, such glory as one might conceive to belong to the "only-begotten" Son of God.

And this glory was "from the Father." You see how he did not say, "and we beheld his glory, glory as of the Word," even though he had said just before, "the Word became flesh." Instead, to teach what kind of Word he held to subsist (not a word that merely signifies something; for how could such a word possibly become flesh?), he necessarily called him Only-begotten.

He also teaches that his glory is the glory by which he is understood to be the only-begotten Son of God, and he says that this glory came to him from nowhere else than "from the Father." For the glory he had was not unbegotten, nor without beginning, nor his own possession; he received it from the Father. He himself made this plain when he said, "Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed."

And the Father answers him, saying, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The same evangelist establishes his subsistence still further when he goes on: "John bears witness about him and cries out, saying, 'This was he who comes after me, who has come to be ahead of me, because he was before me.' For from his fullness we have all received."

But though John cries out that he was before him, the new Sabellius does not hear it. And yet in the flesh John the Baptist preceded the Savior in birth. How, then, does he testify that the Savior came before him? In his birth according to the flesh the Savior was not before him.

Therefore it was as the Only-begotten of God that he was before John and "has come to be ahead of" him. Can these words, then, be referred to the Father and God of the universe, or to a Word in God that has no substance and no subsistence and is the same as God? How could it be possible to say of a Word that does not subsist, "he has come to be ahead of me"? And who would be so mad as to suppose that John the Baptist said of the God of the universe, "he has come to be ahead of me" and "because he was before me"?

So these passages have shown that the one spoken of as God existed before John's birth and came to be ahead of him. And it has been established that before his coming in the flesh he both was and was named not only Word, but also God, Light, and Only-begotten.

5. Where the evangelist gained his knowledge of these things he himself will make clear when he says next, "The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known." You see from whom he learned the theology of the Son.

For it is not Moses who says this, nor any of the prophets after Moses, nor even any of the angels or of the higher powers; it is the only-begotten Son himself who has declared it. So the invisible God did not make the declaration; rather the only-begotten Son, having become visible, gave men the account of the Father, being plainly other than the invisible God. Moreover, he pre-existed not in the mind of the Father, as Marcellus supposed, but in his bosom. Just as the Saviour has promised us that we shall rest in the bosoms of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, so too the Son was in the bosom of the Father. He was not one and the same with the Father, since neither shall we be the same as the holy fathers.

But beyond this, observe how, after he has once named him Word, declared him God, called him light, spoken of him as only-begotten and confessed him Son of God, the evangelist no longer calls him Word. From then on he relates that the Saviour himself calls himself not Word but Son, only-begotten, light, life, truth and countless other things. So we may hear him teaching in this way: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish”; and again, “For God did not send the Son into the world

to judge the world”; and once more, “But whoever does not believe is judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.” Here again God gave and sent the Son as Saviour of the world, while the one who was sent was plainly other than the one who sent him. That is why I think our Saviour himself is recorded in what follows as saying, as if against Marcellus himself and against those who begrudge the Son his nature: “Is it not written in the law, ‘I said, you are gods’?

If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and scripture cannot be broken, do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” You hear how often the Saviour himself named himself not Word but Son, and called himself only-begotten;

how he taught that he had been sent, and had been sanctified by the Father before he was sent; and how he shames those who hesitate to confess him Son of God, teaching from the divine scripture that men who are mortal by nature have been called not only sons of God but even gods. Therefore one must not think it blasphemous to confess as both Son of God and God the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.

What, then, ought to happen to a man who, after so many such sayings, dared to say that he is Word and nothing else, and who said in so many words (Marcellus, fr. 43 = 81 Rettberg): “And for this reason he does not call himself Son of God, but everywhere calls himself Son of Man, so that by such a confession he might enable man, through his fellowship with him, to become son of God by adoption”? Having said this, I do not know with what eyes Marcellus could face, or with what lips he could answer, so many testimonies.

The Saviour also showed that he was light, in agreement with what had already been said about the light, when he said, “I am the light of the world”; and again, “I am the light, and the truth and the life”; and once more, “The light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light.”

And if anyone should ask where he came from, the one who said this will answer: “He who comes from above is above all,” and, “He who comes from heaven bears witness to what he has seen and heard.” But who was it that came from heaven? Surely not the flesh which the Saviour assumed? By no means. Clearly it was he himself, the light and the Word and God and the only-begotten and the Son, he being all these things. It is he, then, who “bears witness,” it says, “to what he has seen and heard.” So he both saw and heard before he came to earth.

And whom did he see but the Father? And whom did he hear but the Father? Thus he taught that he was not a signifying word but a Son truly living and subsisting, so that he says, “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.” Let us believe, then, that the Father, loving the Son, “has given all things into his hand.”

We must pay careful attention to the words “all things,” which embrace the existence of everything that has come into being. Through them one may see the greatness of the power of the Son of God, if one considers how great and what kind of hand it was with which he received from the Father the existence of all things that are.

For if the whole heaven and the world are great, and the things beyond what is seen, which subsist in incorporeal, incorruptible, intellectual and divine powers, are far greater and more excellent still, along with everything that escapes our mind and lies hidden from our knowledge, then the one hand of the only-begotten Son of God, grasping all these things, displays the excellence of his immeasurably great power.

The Son himself showed this again in another saying: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father.” Then, as though we were at a loss as to who and how great he might be who had received so great a trust, he says: do not seek, do not ask. For it is not in its nature to be known by men; indeed, not even the higher and more divine powers have an exact comprehension of the Son of God.

That is why, having first said, “All things have been handed over to me by my Father,” he added, “and no one knows the Son except the Father.” Let every account of the Son of God that is beyond utterance, then, be kept in silence, and let the knowledge of his generation from the Father be left to the Father alone. Let no one press his inquiry further into a nature and essence beyond utterance. Let his own teaching about himself alone be made firm for us by the grace of faith, since it teaches clearly that all things have been handed over to him by the Father.

So God gave and handed over for improvement and benefit, making the handing over as to the Saviour, physician and pilot of the universe; and the Son received, and as a faithful guardian of a trust took charge of the gift, not as an unsubstantial and non-subsistent word, but as being truly the only-begotten and beloved Son of the Father.

7. In addition to this, he called himself the bread of life, saying, “I am the bread of life,” “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” And he made very plain how he was living, setting it out most distinctly where he says, “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father,

so whoever eats me will also live because of me.” He taught this elsewhere too, saying, “For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.” So then he was the bread of life, and he existed in heaven, watering and nourishing the angelic powers by the power of his divinity; and he was all these things before he came to earth, and he was the Son “having life in himself,” just as the Father has “life in himself.”

For the Son alone would possess that which is exceptional and distinctive in the unbegotten and divine life of the Father, on account of which the Father alone is said, according to the divine apostle, to have immortality; for the Son is the image of the Father, and is so in this respect too. Yet he has this life not without beginning, nor unbegotten, nor as his own possession as the Father does, but as received from the Father.

For so it says: “He has granted the Son also to have life in himself, just as the Father has life in himself.” So the one gave, and the other received. And he alone has received this privilege: life is not supplied to him from somewhere outside, as it is to other living beings, but he has it welling up within himself, after the manner of the life that is in the Father. That is why all things that share in life live by the Son’s provision, while he alone has life welling up within himself, the Father having bestowed this on him for the enjoyment of those who were to be made alive through him.

He himself teaches this when he says, “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven.” You see how even when he was in heaven he was the bread of life. That is why it is said somewhere, “Man ate the bread of angels.” So even before he was sent by the Father he was in heaven and lived because of the Father,
not as a signifying word, nor as being one and the same with God, but as subsisting and having a life of his own, which the Father has given him.

And going on further, showing the surpassing glory of the Father, he said, “As the Father taught me, so I speak. And he who sent me is with me; he has not left me alone, for I always do what is pleasing to him.” Note carefully how the word “always” is used.

For, he says, it is not only now, while I converse with men on earth through the flesh, that I do what is pleasing to the Father, but always. He also testifies that he speaks what he has learned from the Father as from a teacher. So he names the Father as his teacher, being plainly other than him, since everyone who is taught by someone is other than the one who teaches.

But if the Word was in God, the Word by which God might also be called rational, being something that signifies the Father’s thoughts, how could he become his own teacher? How could he say he had been sent, if he was inseparable from God? And how could he testify that he did what was pleasing to God, if he was one and the same with God? And if Marcellus should reply to this that the Word spoke these words while in the flesh, what shall we say this has to do with refusing to confess that he is Son, and calling him Word only?

And in what way was he in the flesh when he said these things? Was it as living and subsisting and existing outside the Father? Then what was the Father at that time, if he did not possess his own Word within himself, but subsisted without a Word? And if the Word, dwelling in the flesh while he spent his time on earth, was outside the Father, living and subsisting and moving the flesh as a soul does, he was plainly other than the Father, and once again he and the Father were two hypostases,

and all of Marcellus’ labour is exposed as futile, since he defines the Word who came to be in the flesh as an essential Word, living and subsisting. But if the Word dwelling in the body was outside God, and yet was united and joined to God so as to be one and the same with him, he must necessarily grant one of these: either that it was the Father himself who was in the flesh; or that it was the Son, subsisting by himself and acting in the body; or that it was a human soul; or, if none of these, that the flesh, soulless and irrational, moved of its own accord.

If he says it was the Father, then for him it will be the Father who was born and suffered and underwent every human experience. It was for saying exactly this that the church of God indicted Sabellius for impiety. But if it is not right to say that the Father became man, then his disciples must confess that it was the Son, as he teaches.

And if Marcellus denies that the Son subsists, it is time to suppose that Christ was a mere man, composed of body and soul, so as to differ in no way from the common nature of men. But this doctrine too has been driven out of the church. Those who held it, the Ebionites long ago and more recently the man from Samosata and those called Paulianists after him, have suffered the punishment due to blasphemers.

What then remains after this, except to introduce the flesh alone, without any indweller, moving like the automata of the conjurers? And how could the flesh, the body by itself without anything acting in it, have said, “As he taught me, so I speak”? How could the flesh have said, “For I always do what is pleasing to him”? How could the flesh say that it had been sent by the Father? And is it reverent to call God the Father of the flesh, rather than of the one who dwelt and acted in it? Who, then, was this? Was it the Word in God, being God himself, as Sabellius holds? Or, as it is reverent and true to say, was it the living and subsisting only-begotten Son of God?

But if he says neither of these, he will necessarily posit a human soul, and Christ will be for him a mere man; and our new writer will no longer be a Sabellian but a Paulianist. And if he should say that the Word in God, being nothing other than a word, a signifying or active word, dwelt in the flesh,

how could this word have said that it lived a life of its own distinct from the Father? How was it sent, if it was always joined and united to God? How does it say that the Father is its teacher? How did it say that it always did what was pleasing to the Father? For these would expressly be the words of a subsisting and living Son. And throughout the whole Gospel, the one who prays to the Father, who glorifies the Father, who asks to be glorified by the Father, what else does he show but that he himself subsists, especially when he says, “The testimony of two men is true.

I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me”? Having shown himself to be living by so many sayings, the Saviour himself nowhere named himself Word, but Son and light and only-begotten and bread of life, and anything rather than Word.

He teaches that he has a word, saying, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word,” but he does not say that he himself is the Word. How then, after all this, does the man who declared that he is Word only and nothing else not blush? Listen to how he wrote: “So it is clear from every side that no other name befits the eternity of the Word than this one, which the most holy disciple and apostle of God, John, spoke at the beginning of the Gospel.”
And again, to show that if there is any new and more recent name, it belonged to him from the new and recent economy according to the flesh.

And once more: “So before he came down and was born through the Virgin, he was Word only. For what else, before it took up human flesh, was that which came down ‘in the last days,’ as he himself wrote, and was born of the Virgin? It was nothing other than Word.”

So much Marcellus is free to say and to declare, because he does not confess the Son of God. To him the evangelist might well cry out loudly: What are you saying, man? I did not call him Word only, but also God, and “the light that enlightens every man coming into the world,” and the “only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father.”

Let no one, then, misrepresent the theologian, but let him listen carefully to what kind of Word he set forth, adding immediately, “and the Word was God,” and further, “all things came into being through him.” And according to the Saviour of the universe himself, he was not once named Word, but Son of God and only-begotten and light and life and truth, and anything rather than Word.

8. And if he should say that these things were spoken in the New Testament, he will be told that “In the beginning was the Word” also comes from nowhere else but from it. It is one and the same Gospel, and the same evangelist who called him Word also wrote all the rest about him.

9. And Paul the divine apostle, when he says, “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things,” clearly names the Son of God who existed before his coming in the flesh, through whom all things came into being, not Word but Lord Jesus and Christ. But if, as Marcellus holds, God and the Word in him were one and the same, it would have been enough for the apostle to say, “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things.”

For the thought would have been complete and the statement self-sufficient in presenting God as maker of the universe. But even a Jew might say this. The herald of the church, however, teaches us not to be ignorant of the second point as well as the first.

And what was this? “And one Lord, Jesus Christ.” So he adds the second point next, saying, “for us” (for even if not for all, yet for us, he says) “one Lord, Jesus Christ.” And why he too, after the one God, is “one Lord” for us, he shows by adding “through whom are all things.” For since “all things came into being through him,” it is fitting that we who know this should believe him to be Lord of the universe after the God who is over all.

That he said this not about the flesh but about God the Word is clear from his adding “through whom are all things.” For he says, “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” This same thing was said both of the light and of the pre-existent Word. So Jesus Christ himself was the light and the Word through whom all things came into being, and not the flesh. For he would not have said “through whom are all things” of the flesh, so incongruously.

10. The same Paul knows how to call the Son of God, who existed before the flesh, Christ, and in the same way he calls him rock, in what he writes about those who spent time with Moses in the wilderness: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” And he sets his seal on the same point further on, saying, “Let us not put Christ to the test, as some of them tested him and were destroyed by the serpents.”

And he confirms this still further when he says, “By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, considering the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt.” And he establishes it more clearly still when he says, “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in fashion as a man.”

You see that before he emptied himself and took the form of a servant, he was, and pre-existed, and was in the form of God. And who was this? None other than Jesus Christ. So he himself, Jesus Christ, was God the Word even before he took flesh.

For we must listen carefully to the divine apostle when he says, “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus,” and then makes clear who this Jesus Christ was by what he adds: “who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

Can the saying be taken to refer to the flesh here too? Is it fitting to say “who” [?] and “being” of the flesh? Did the flesh empty itself, taking the form of a servant? That would be absurd. Come, then, let us examine how it is said: “who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself.” If he was a word without real existence, in no way subsisting outside God but being inside him, sometimes in rest and silence and sometimes in activity,

how could he be “in the form of God,” when he was in potency [God] [?] God himself? How could he “not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,” when he was himself God? And how did he humble himself by becoming obedient to the Father? For one obeying another would indicate two persons.

And since Marcellus has used the word in man as an image, we must ask whether it could fit the human word to say: “who, being in the form of man, did not count equality with man a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, becoming obedient to the man.” How could the word that is inborn in a man do these things, being one and the same with the man? So it will not be a mere and non-subsistent word, but the truly only-begotten Son of God who is “in the form of God,” who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” Him the divine apostle also called Jesus Christ, knowing well that he existed before the flesh.

11. In addition to this, the same apostle called him the mediator of God, saying that the legislation of Moses had been given into his hand, in the words, “The law was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one.” You hear how he speaks of God in his own right and names the angels, and brings in the mediator between them, saying, “Now a mediator is not of one.” So even before he became man, in the time of Moses, he was acting as mediator of the legislation.
12. The same apostle also calls him high priest, saying, “Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God.”

13. More than that, he knows the same one as radiance of the glory and stamp of God, and as Son and heir, when he says, “In these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages; who, being the radiance of his glory and the stamp of his hypostasis.” And here (just as it was said above of the Word, “all things came into being through him,” and of the light, “he was in the world, and the world came into being through him,” and of Jesus Christ, “for us there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things”)
see how “through whom he also made the ages” is said in the same way of the same one.

14. Here it is worth paying attention to how he is named radiance. For I think the term indicates the Son’s generation from the Father. Since he has often been named Son, and God has been called Father, the apostle has used an image more fitting for God, so that we might not sink down to the begetting of animals and imagine something of that sort,

For he said of the Father that he "dwells in unapproachable light," and defined the Son as the radiance of the Father's light, so that the radiance is the offspring of the first light. It did not come into being in the way that mortal animals are born, but after the manner of the example he gave. It is fitting, then, that he also calls him "the image of the invisible God," because he exists "in the form of God" and because he is "the radiance" and "the exact imprint of his substance."

For this reason, writing about him, he said: "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; for in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through him and for him; and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together."

These words were spoken about the divinity of the Son of God, whatever Marcellus may think. The divine apostle would not have said so much about the flesh. That would be foolish and unintelligible, besides making the wording incoherent. How would it have been fitting to say of the flesh "who is the image"? He would have had to say, if anything, "which is the image."

15. And elsewhere the same apostle again called him the image of God, saying: "And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that the light of the gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, may not shine in their hearts."

Here we should note that the divine apostle gave a definition of Christ when he called him the image of God, so that no one would suppose that there are two gods, but only one, who is over all. For if there is one God, and there is no other besides him, it would be he who is made known through the Son, as through an image.

This is why the Son too is God: because the Father is given form in him as in an image. The divine apostle shows this, at one time saying, "who, being in the form of God," and at another defining him as the image of God. So, along with his other titles, the Son both was and was called the image of God before his coming in the flesh. But these few passages, out of countless others, we have collected from the New Testament for the sake of keeping our discussion within bounds.

16. The prophets of God who lived long ago also honored the same one with various divine titles. One called him the Spirit of God, saying: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from the root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding," and so on. By these words he clearly indicated the one who was of the seed of David according to the flesh, and God the Word who dwelt in him. Hence the divine apostle at one time said, "Now the Lord is the Spirit," and at another, "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." Another prophet likewise calls him spirit, saying, "The spirit before our face, Christ the Lord." And in the Gospel it is clearly said of him: "Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased. I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations."

17. Another of the prophets named him life and light when he addressed God and said, "For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light." For what was the fountain of life and the light that is with God, if not the one who said in the Gospels, "I am the light of the world," and "I am the way and the truth and the life"? That is why the prophet, again supplicating God in prayer, says: "Send out your light and your truth; they will lead me."

18. Zerubbabel, too, called him truth, and was judged worthy of the prize for it. It is recorded that before the king of the Persians he said: "And truth endures and is strong forever, and lives and prevails forever and ever. With her there is no partiality, but she does what is just and keeps away from everything unjust and wicked." To this he adds: "And hers is the strength and the kingdom and the authority and the majesty of all the ages." By saying that truth lives and conquers and prevails, he very vividly showed that it has real existence. In keeping with this, the Savior himself, when he named himself the truth, set his seal on Zerubbabel's testimony.
19. He was also named a river by the one who said, "The streams of the river make glad the city of God."

20. And he was also called a mountain by the one who said, "The mountain in which God was pleased to dwell." This is why, in Daniel, he was seen as a stone cut from a mountain without hands, and again the same stone was seen being turned into a high mountain. The mountain signifies the preexistence of his divinity, and the stone his humanity.
21. They also called him righteousness, as did the one who said, "Who has raised up righteousness from the east?"

22. And the sun of righteousness, as did the one who said, "But for those who fear me the sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings." And another says, "The sun shall set upon the prophets who lead my people astray." These words would certainly not fit the visible sun, nor indeed the Word in the flesh.

23. Solomon in Proverbs also names him wisdom, saying, "Wisdom has built herself a house and set up seven pillars," and so on. And he taught that Wisdom existed before the world, living and subsisting, by uttering these words in her person: "I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling, and I have called upon knowledge and understanding." Then he goes on to add: "Through me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just; through me great men are made great, and through me sovereigns hold sway."
24. Solomon also called him the tree of life and Lord, saying, "She is a tree of life to all who lay hold of her, and for those who lean on her, as on the Lord, she is secure."

25. And Solomon's father, David, in the Psalms named him both Lord and priest: at one time saying, "The Lord said to my Lord, 'Sit at my right hand,'" and at another declaring, "The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: 'You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.'"

26. The same David also knows to confess him as God, saying: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." For who else could this God be, who is anointed by God, than the very one who was proclaimed Christ because of the Father's anointing?
27. This same one was also the beloved of God, as the title of the psalm shows, which reads: "A song for the beloved."
28. Isaiah called him an arm, saying: "The Lord will reveal his holy arm before all the nations."
29. And David knew him as both righteousness and salvation, which is why he said: "The Lord has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness before the nations,"
and again, "Proclaim his salvation from day to day," and once more, "Who will give the salvation of Israel out of Zion?" and "Show us your mercy, O Lord, and grant us your salvation."

30. But why should I go through each of these one by one, when anyone eager to learn can gather such passages from the whole of divinely inspired Scripture?
