Through it the men of God are seen to have been enlightened by the divine Spirit with the knowledge of the only-begotten Son of God, a knowledge that was secret at that time and hidden from the multitudes of the Jewish people. That is why they spoke of him in various ways, using veiled titles. For the grace of proclaiming the doctrine of his divinity was being reserved for his coming; and his Church throughout the whole world, having received it as a mystery long hidden and kept in silence, takes pride in it.

The divine apostle teaches this very thing when he says: "according to the stewardship of God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations, but now revealed to his saints. To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory." You see how the mystery that was previously hidden but has now been revealed is the Son of God.

So the prophets of God, by the prophetic Spirit, spoke of his divinity in a hidden way, while the mass of the Jewish nation remained ignorant of the hidden mystery. Hence that nation was taught to know one God, because it was constantly being drawn away into the error of many gods, but it did not know that God is the Father of an only-begotten Son. For this mystery was being kept for the Church of the Gentiles,

given to her as a special grace, for in him, as the apostle says, "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." So through all these passages the Word of God, who "in the beginning was with God," has been shown not to have been called only Word, as Marcellus thinks, but also Son and Only-begotten, light and bread, Jesus and Christ and Lord, high priest, radiance, imprint and image, firstborn of all creation, fountain of life, truth, river, righteousness, sun of righteousness, wisdom, tree of life, Lord and God, beloved, priest, arm, righteousness and salvation. He was all these things, and was called by these names while he existed before the flesh, as the scriptures we have cited have shown.

Why, then, does Marcellus pass over all these and fix on the Word alone, refusing to go on to the other titles and asserting that he is only the Word of God, and a word that merely signifies, at one time resting quietly in God, at another speaking, saying or doing things by activity alone? Is it not because he is an outright Sabellian, and does not believe in the Son of God, nor recognize the mystery that existed long ago but has been revealed to the Church of Christ alone through his grace?

But suppose he should say that the unknown mystery was that God has a word within himself and makes use of a word. (This is what Marcellus himself thinks, for he writes as follows: "For what other hidden mystery was there than the one concerning the Word? This mystery was formerly so hidden in God that none of the former people clearly knew the things concerning the Word.") If, then, he should say this, let him learn that any Jew who has not recognized the Christ of God would also admit that God has a word and is not without reason.

Sabellius himself, too, and every Greek and barbarian who holds that God exists, would say this without dispute. For as soon as one says "God," one thinks of him as wise, rational, powerful, just and good. What sort of hidden mystery, then, was this, when everyone admits it? Who would not say that in God there are wisdom and power and life and light and truth and righteousness and reason, and everything noble and good? Or rather, that he himself is all these things, and whatever is higher and better than these and unknown to us? For self-taught nature compels every human being to confess these things about God. Hence we are taught that the Son too is all these things,

since he is the only-begotten Son and heir of the Father, and has everything that the Father has. That is why he is said to be in the form of God and the image of God, according to the divine apostle, who said, "who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped," and again, "who is the image of God."

So the fact that God is rational was not "the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations," nor was something known to all human beings by their natural understanding only now revealed. But if anyone should ask what the mystery was, the apostle answers, saying, "but now revealed to his saints. To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you."

Christ, then, was the mystery, that is, clearly, the Son of God. That is why the prophets of God formerly glorified him in a hidden way with various titles, concealing what was not to be spoken and reserving its revelation to all for his own grace. So when, after so many testimonies from the scriptures, Marcellus insists that the Word who was in the beginning was nothing other than Word before he took on flesh, and bore no other name, but received his various titles only when "the Word became flesh," having been nothing but Word before that, how could he not be convicted of being ignorant and without understanding of the divine scriptures? But now that this has been established, come, let us look at the new Sabellius, as though he had come back to life.

After the testimonies we have cited from the divine scriptures, which showed that before his coming in the flesh the Son of God was named not only Word (as Marcellus thought) but countless other things as well, come now, let us look at the ghost of Sabellius, as it rises up, so to speak, out of the earth. Marcellus, then, dared to say that the very God who is over all, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, was born of the holy Virgin and himself suffered. He writes as follows: "What, then, was it that came down before the incarnation? Spirit, surely," he says. "For if one should want to say anything other than this, the angel who said to the Virgin, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you,' will not allow it. But if he says it was spirit, let him listen to the Savior saying, 'God is spirit.'"

In these words he said that the spirit that came upon the Virgin was the God of the universe, of whom our Savior and Lord taught, saying, "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth." In this he openly revives Sabellius.

And going on further, when Jeremiah the prophet speaks plainly about the Savior's becoming human, "Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among men," Marcellus refers the saying to the Father, stating in so many words: "But it seems that the Father is in the Word, even if Asterius and those who think as he does disagree."

He does the same with the Savior's passion. Citing from Jeremiah's Lamentations the words, "The spirit of our face, Christ the Lord, was taken in their corruptions," he adds here likewise: "The prophet is speaking of the Word who took on our flesh." And he goes on to say: "A spirit could never produce a shadow. But that God himself is spirit, the Savior said: 'God is spirit.' And that God is light, he himself teaches us, saying, 'I am the light.'" You see how he transfers what was said about the Savior to the divinity of the Father.

And again he brazenly abolishes the real existence of the Son, declaring that before the creation of things that came into being there was nothing else except God alone. He writes, word for word, as follows: "Asterius calls the authority given to him glory, and not only glory but glory before the world, not realizing that before the world had come into being there was nothing else except God alone." And again he confirms the same point, saying: "Heaven and earth and all things in heaven and on earth have been made by God. If, then, he believes this, he must also admit that there was nothing else except God."

You see a man who, like a Jew, openly denies the only-begotten Son of God, through whom all things came into being. For if there was nothing else except God before the creation of the world, then the Son did not exist. And how, then, did "all things come into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being"? The Jew who denies the Christ of God knows of nothing before the creation of the world except God alone, and Marcellus bears witness with him. But the Church of Christ takes pride, with all boldness, in saying: "For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things."

When she says "through whom are all things," she knows that he existed before all things. So whoever says that before the creation of the world there was nothing else except God alone is speaking falsely against the truth. For along with the only God, his only-begotten Son also existed before the founding of the world, and was with the Father. This is what she was taught by the one who said, "In these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages."

And in Proverbs, through Solomon, the Son himself teaches about himself, saying, "When he was preparing the heavens, I was present with him." Moreover, he himself was "the light that enlightens every man coming into the world," since "he was in the world, and the world came into being through him." And if "the world came into being through him," it is clear that he existed before the world.

So God was not alone before the founding of the world; his only-begotten Son was with him. The Father looked upon him and rejoiced, as the Son himself, being Wisdom, teaches, saying in Proverbs, "I was the one in whom he delighted daily." And the Son himself, gazing intently on the Father's thoughts, was filled with gladness, which is why he says, "And I rejoiced before him at all times." These are the holy and divine mysteries that the Church of Christ has received and guards. But whoever says that before the world had come into being there was nothing else except God alone

shows himself to be one of two things: either a Jew or a Sabellian. For either he denies the Son outright and introduces God alone, and so will be a Jew denying the Christ; or he accepts the title of Son only as far as the word goes, while asserting that he is the one God, Son and Father at once, and so will revive Sabellius. For if there was nothing else except God before the world, then either God himself will be both Father and Son, or he will have no Son at all.

But it seems that Marcellus says the Son is the word within God himself, by virtue of which God is understood to be rational; so that God would be his own father, and in turn his own son. Listen, at any rate, to his own words, in which he writes as follows: "For before all creation there was, as is fitting, a kind of stillness, since the Word was in God.

For if Asterius has believed that God is the maker of all things, it is clear that he too will agree with us that God has always existed and never received a beginning of his being, while the things that exist were made by him, and made out of nothing." You see how, having posited that God is without beginning, he said that the Word, being in him, was in stillness before creation. And going on further he adds: "If, then, he believes this, he must also admit that there was nothing else except God. The Word, then, had his own glory, being in the Father."

Hence, consistently enough, he says that the Word is eternal, that is, unbegotten, writing as follows: "Do you hear, then, the harmony of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness through many different persons to the eternity of the Word?" And again: "And for this reason he begins from the eternity of the Word, saying, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' By using three successive testimonies he means to show the eternity of the Word."

How he claimed that the Word is united with God and is unbegotten together with him, one can hear from his own words, where he says something like this: "We know that the dispensation according to the flesh belongs to the man, but we have believed that the eternity according to the spirit is united with the Father."

Having granted in this way that the Word is in God, he goes on to declare that the Word is one and the same with him, writing word for word as follows: "For if the spirit alone were examined, the Word would reasonably appear to be one and the same with God; but if the addition of the flesh in the Savior's case were examined, the Godhead seems to be expanded by activity alone; so that it is reasonably a truly indivisible monad."

And again, going on, he says: "It is not, then, because of their exact agreement in all words and deeds, as Asterius said, that the Savior says, 'I and the Father are one,' but because it is impossible for either the Word of God or God to be divided from his own Word." If, then, God and the Word in him were one and the same, as Marcellus thinks, then the one who came to be in the holy Virgin, was made flesh, became human, suffered what is recorded, and died for our sins was the very God who is over all. When Sabellius dared to say this, the Church of God counted him among the godless and blasphemers.

And if Marcellus should say that it was the Word of God who was made flesh, he nevertheless defined him as inseparable [?] from God, granting an indivisible monad and a single subsistence of God and the Word in him, so that, according to him, the one who became human is to be understood as none other than the God who is over all. But if it is an indivisible monad, and God and the Word in him are one and the same, whom could one call Father and whom Son, when there is only one underlying subject? In this way, then, Marcellus, by introducing one and the same being as Son-Father, revived Sabellius.

The church of God, however, both acknowledges the undivided unity, confessing one first principle, the one God who is unbegotten and without beginning, and also names as Savior the only-begotten Son who was begotten from him, who truly exists, lives and subsists. It does not hold that he is without beginning or unbegotten, so as not to posit two first principles and two gods; rather, he was begotten from the Father himself and has as his beginning the one who begot him.

That is why the church has received the faith to believe in one God, the Father Almighty, and in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, since this holy and mystical faith grants rebirth in Christ to those who are enlightened through it. But Marcellus says that the unity is expanded by activity. That has a place where bodies are concerned, but not where the bodiless, unspeakable and inexpressible being is concerned.

For God is not expanded when he acts, nor contracted when he does not act. He does not act at all as human beings do, nor does he move as they do. Being an undivided unity, God begot his only-begotten Son from himself without being divided and without undergoing any alteration, change, flux or passion.

For when he commands, gives orders or makes laws, he does not do these things by speaking with tongue and lips as human beings do. Nor, when he looks upon the ordering of the universe, does he gaze at it using eyes as we do, since by an unspeakable and divine power he anticipates even the things that do not yet exist and beholds them as though they already existed and subsisted.

Nor, when he makes and fashions things, does he take pre-existing matter and work it with hands and fingers as our craftsmen do. Again, by an unspeakable and incomprehensible power he brought the substance of all created things out of nonexistence into being. If, then, he made all things by means that are unspeakable and beyond our reasoning, why should we worry that we might be saying that, as with mortal living creatures, some passion befell him in begetting the Son? He brought the Son into being above all things and before all things, not in any way known to mortal nature, but in a manner known to him alone.

But are you afraid, sir, that by confessing two hypostases you will introduce two first principles and fall away from the monarchy of the Godhead? Learn, then, that since there is one God without beginning and unbegotten, and the Son has been begotten from him, there will be one first principle, one monarchy and one kingdom, since the Son himself also names his own Father as his first principle. For "the head of Christ is God," according to the apostle.

Or are you anxious that whoever confesses that there are two hypostases, of Father and of Son, must accept two gods? Then understand this too: whoever grants two hypostases, of Father and of Son, is not compelled to speak of two fathers or of two sons. He will grant that the one is Father and the other Son. In the same way, then, whoever posits the two hypostases is not compelled to grant two gods.

For we do not define them as equal in honor, nor both as without beginning and unbegotten. One is unbegotten and without beginning; the other is begotten and has the Father as its beginning. That is why the Son himself also teaches that his own Father is his God too, when he says: "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God."
So God the Father is shown to be the God even of the Son himself.

For this reason one God is proclaimed by the church of the Son. When the Son himself is compared with the Father, he will no longer be God of the Father himself, but his only-begotten and beloved Son, "the image of the invisible God" and "the radiance" of the Father's "glory." He reveres, worships and glorifies his own Father, naming him as his own God as well. It is recorded that he prayed to him, gave thanks to him, and became obedient to him "to the point of death."

He also confesses that he lives because of the Father, that he can do nothing apart from the Father, and that he does not do his own will but the Father's. Indeed he says in so many words: "I have come down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me"; and again: "I can do nothing of myself. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will but the will of him who sent me." And he shows that the one who sent him was other than himself when he goes on to say: "If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true;

there is another who testifies about me." Then, after mentioning the Baptist, he teaches that the Father is his witness, saying: "And the Father who sent me has himself testified about me." And he adds: "If you loved me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, because my Father is greater than I."

Through all these sayings he shows that he is other than the Father. And he sets forth the surpassing glory of the Father by saying that the Father sent him, while he himself was sent and came down from heaven not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him. What could Marcellus say to this, when he hears the one who came down from heaven teaching these things? Surely he will not claim in this case too that it is the Savior's flesh saying these things, for the flesh did not come down from heaven.

Whom, then, will he say it was who came down from heaven and taught these things? God himself, or the Word united with him? If he says it was the Father, openly unveiling his Sabellianism, the Savior himself will refute him as a liar when he says: "I have come down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me,"

and "I can do nothing of myself. As I hear, I judge," and "I do not seek my own will but the will of him who sent me," and "My Father is greater than I." To suppose that the Father says these things would be the height of madness.

But if he says that it is the Word that is inherent in God—his mind, by which he reasons and thinks inwardly within himself—that speaks the words before us, then how could God's thought and the mind within him have come down from heaven? How could it, having come to be in the flesh it assumed, have spoken these words? And how will the Word that is in God say that he came down not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him?

By these words, then, the Son of God sets forth his own reverence toward the Father. But when he is set at the head of all the begotten things that came into being through him, as the Savior, Lord and Creator of them all (for "all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being"), then he may be proclaimed God, Master, Savior and King.
That is why his church has been taught to revere, worship and honor him as God, having learned to do this from him.

The Savior himself says: "For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father." He expressly commands that he be honored not as the prophets are, nor as the angels or the powers that excel them, but in the same way as the Father himself. For the Father himself, willing this, "has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor him just as they honor the Father."

Thomas called Didymus, who knew these things precisely, being one of the company of the twelve disciples, named him in shining words both God and Lord, saying: "My Lord and my God." That is why it is fitting for us too to revere the Son alone, and no one else, with divine honor, just as we honor the Father. And in this the Father is honored through the Son,

as he himself teaches when he says: "Whoever honors the Son honors the Father who sent him." For just as, when we honor an image of a king that has been sent out, we would be honoring the king himself, the original of the image, in the same way the Father would be honored through the Son, since he is also seen through him.

For "whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father," beholding the unbegotten Godhead expressed in the Son as in an image and a mirror. For he is "a radiance of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness." All these things he has received from the Father, and he holds the glory of the Godhead as received from him, as his genuine and only-begotten Son. But the Father has not received anything from anyone; being himself the first principle, source and root of all good things, he may rightly be proclaimed the one and only God.

But Marcellus, being ignorant of these things, does not want the Son to have been truly begotten from the Father as a living and subsisting Son. He says instead that he came forth from God as a word that signifies something or gives a command. Hear him saying this openly in these words: "To say that he was begotten before the ages seems to have been said consistently, for what has come forth becomes the offspring of the father who sent it forth. But the other point he no longer takes up soundly or piously. For to say that the one who came forth from him is not the Word, and that this is not the true mode of generation, but that he is truly Son only, tends to present hearers with an impression of something seen in human terms."

Then, to establish that the Word was not even begotten from the Father, he says word for word: "So the holy apostle and disciple of the Lord, John, recalling his eternity, became a true witness to the Word when he said, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,' making no mention here of any generation of the Word." In this way, denying the Son of God, he claimed that the Word in God was at one time within God, at another time came forth from God, and at another time again will run back up into God and be in him,

just as he was before. Listen to how he says this in these words: "But now I believe the divine Scriptures, that God is one, and that his Word came forth from the Father so that all things might come into being through him. But after the time of judgment, the setting right of all things and the destruction of every opposing power, 'then he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him,' to God and the Father, so that the Word may thus be in God just as he was before the world existed. For since nothing existed before except God alone, and all things were to come into being through the Word, the Word came forth by an effective activity, being the Word of the Father."

And again he sets out the same idea more plainly, writing as follows: "For before the world existed the Word was in the Father. But when God Almighty purposed to make all things in heaven and on earth, the coming into being of the world required an effective activity. And for this reason, since nothing else existed except God (for it is agreed that all things came into being by him), the Word then came forth and became the maker of the world, he who had also previously been preparing it inwardly in thought."

And again, after all this, he goes on to say: "And for this reason he does not call himself Son of God, but everywhere calls himself Son of Man, so that by such a confession he might prepare man to become son of God by adoption through communion with him, and after the completion of his work might again, as Word, be united with God, fulfilling what the apostle said: 'Then he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.' For then he will be what he was before." Having said this much about the Word in God, by which we understand God to be rational, Marcellus has fallen into a terrible difficulty, having dared to say that the Word in God was at one time outside God, and will again be within him after the time of judgment, so that he may thus be in God, united with him, just as he was before.

It is time, then, for him to answer our questions. What should we think about the intervening time, when the Word was outside God? How did he come forth? And in what condition was God, then, when he did not have his own Word within himself? For if at the consummation of the universe the Word will be in God just as he was before, prior to the time of the consummation, how will it be the Word that came forth from God? If he came to subsist by himself as other than God, Marcellus's labor is in vain. But if, even when he came forth from God, he remained inseparable from the Father, like the uttered word in us, then he was always and continually in God, even when he was acting.

How, then, can he defer it to the time of judgment, saying that he will then be united with God and will be just as he was before? For if he will then be as he was before, not only will the Word that came forth from God not be as he was before, but God himself will be unlike himself: once having the Word within himself, and at the consummation of the universe receiving him back and becoming then just as he was before, while in the intervening time being in a different condition. And the Word likewise, having come to be outside God, will not be what he was before until the consummation of the universe.

And what doctrine could be more impious than this? For "was" and "will be," "once came to be" and "will be again," all indicate change in time, and would be foreign to the being that is timeless, without beginning, uncreated and unchangeable. Of that being we may properly conceive only that it is, and that it always is invariably the same and remains in the same state: not diminished, not contracted, not extended, not unfolded, having nothing outside or inside itself, not becoming different at different times, not being one thing first and then becoming something else and then being restored to its original state.

Yet these are the very things Marcellus dared to propose. He says that God existed of old, and imagines for himself a kind of stillness together with God, following that founder of the godless heretics who, teaching godless doctrines, declared: "There was God and Silence." Then, he says, after the silence and stillness, the Word of God came forth at the beginning of the making of the world by an effective activity, so that he was no longer as he had been before, at rest in the silent God, but came forth from God and acted. And how, then, did he come forth?

Surely by the utterance of an articulate voice, with God evidently speaking and talking as human beings do. This, at any rate, was his view, for he writes as follows: "For just as all things that have come into being have come into being by the Father through the Word, so too the things spoken by the Father are signified through the Word."

And again: "For whatever the Father says, he is seen everywhere to say it through the Word. This is clear from our own case as well, so far as small things may be compared with great and divine ones. For we too do everything we wish to say and do, as far as we can, by our own word."

If, then, the Word came forth from the Father in this way, by an effective activity, how did it occur to Marcellus to set a limit to the Word's activity at the time of the consummation, when he says that the Word will be in God just as he was before? (And before, by his account, he was at rest in the silent God.) So after the consummation there will also be a kind of stillness, with the Word no longer going to act. "But before the formation of created things," he says, "there was nothing except God, and since there was nothing, he reasonably assigned stillness to himself."

But for the time of the consummation the prophet Daniel foretells that there will be myriads before the throne of God, saying: "A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him."

And then, surely, all the sons of the age to come will be there: the blessed souls of patriarchs, prophets and apostles, the holy spirits of martyrs, and all the sheep of our Savior, who will stand at his right hand and hear: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world."

Since, then, so many will exist and live an immortal life after the time of judgment, why will the Word of God not be active then too? Where did Marcellus get the idea of declaring that God will then no longer speak to the saints or make use of his active Word, but will be as he was before, evidently silent and at rest in himself? For this is what he established by saying many times that he will then be as he was before; and before, as he himself said, he was in stillness.

So God will then fall silent. Before that he spoke and used his Word as active, but then, in the very kingdom of heaven that was promised, he will deprive his saints of his own Word and of the wisdom in him. Do you see to what a precipice he has gone, having used no guide, not even the divine Scriptures? All this, at any rate, he has put together for himself from a single expression which he did not understand.

For as soon as he turned to the proofs from the new and fresh covenant, he found himself hemmed in and driven back on every side. Finding only one expression that supported his false doctrine, he seized on it alone as if he had stumbled on a windfall—and even that was spoken not in the person of our Savior but in the person of the evangelist, in which he named him, saying: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Starting from this, he denied the Son, as though he were nothing other than a word like the one we know among ourselves.

Yet the great and divine evangelist himself did not call him Word only, as we have often said, but also God, light, Son and Only-begotten. And he records that the Savior himself nowhere in Scripture called himself Word, but throughout the Gospel called himself life, light, the only-begotten, the Son of God, truth, resurrection, bread of life, vine, shepherd and countless other things, as has already been shown.

Why, then, when there are so many names, does he not stop at the literal wording in all the others but search out the meaning of what is said, while in the case of "Word" alone he says that the term is used of him in its proper sense, as if he were nothing other than a word? He writes in these very words: "He was not called Word by a loose usage—even if those who teach otherwise burst with their lies—but is properly and truly Word."

And again: "Let him learn, then, that the Word of God has come, not a Word called so by loose usage, as they say, but one that is truly Word." And again: "Before, as I have often said, he was nothing other than Word." (Marcellus, fragment 43 = 81 Rettberg.) And again: "Before he came down and was born through the Virgin, he was Word only. For what else was it, before it took on human flesh, that came down 'in the last days,' as he himself wrote, and was born of the Virgin? It was nothing other than Word." When Marcellus says this, it would be right to put a question like this to him: "Where, my good man,

do you get this addition of 'nothing other' and 'only'? We know precisely that 'in the beginning was the Word.' And not only that, but also that 'the Word was God,' and that he was 'the light that enlightens every person,' and that he was the only-begotten Son, and all the other things that have been listed. But that he was Word only and nothing other than Word, no one could show to have been said anywhere."

Where, then, does this daring addition come from? Why should one not rather say that he is Son only and nothing other than Son? Why not God and nothing other than God? Why not the light of the world and nothing other than that? Why not life and nothing other? And one could quite rightly put the same question about similar titles.

But just as anyone who said this would be proven wrong (for he is all these things at once, being the one Son of God and whatever is higher than these, having been deemed worthy of the various titles according to each aspect of the divine powers in him),

so too in the case of "Word," whoever says that he is Word only and nothing other would rightly be said to be mistaken. Only the evangelist John called him Word, and not only that but other things as well, while the Savior called himself light, truth, life, only-begotten Son and the rest, but never Word. How, then, is it not absurd to refrain from saying, in the case of the names he gave himself, that he is one of them and nothing other, and yet, in the case of the evangelist's expression about him that calls him Word, to insist that he was nothing other than Word?

"But he is properly and truly Word," he says. Why then is he not properly and truly God? It was not one person who called him Word and another who called him God. One and the same evangelist taught that he was both God and Word together, saying, "and the Word was God," and the same evangelist also named him light. Why, then, is he not properly and truly only-begotten Son, and all the other things to which the Master and Savior himself has testified about himself through the evangelist? But Marcellus passes over all these and says that he is properly and truly Word only. And he adds that he was Word only, and from there he falls into likening him to a human word.

When he hears him called light, he does not fall into thinking of bodily light, nor does he say that he is like the radiance of the sun. Yet in the case of "Word" he presents him as something that signifies, and as like the human word. So he says that at one time he is at rest in God and at another he goes forth from God, and that he comes to be both within him and outside him, after the likeness of the word in us, both the one called "internal" and the one heard when it is uttered by the voice.

He says, then, in these very words: "For whatever the Father says, he is everywhere seen to say through the Word. This is clear also from our own case, so far as small things may be compared with great and divine ones: for we too do by our own word whatever we wish to say and do, so far as we are able." And again he says this: "For before all creation there was, as is likely, a kind of silence, since the Word was in God." Then he adds: "For since nothing existed before except God alone, and all things were about to come into being through the Word, the Word came forth by active energy."

Having said this much about the Word, listen to how he tries to interpret the words of the Gospel, writing as follows: "But the holy apostle and disciple of the Lord, John, teaching clearly and expressly at the beginning of the Gospel, as of something previously unknown among men, and naming him the Word of the Almighty, spoke thus: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' Not using just one testimony, he signifies the eternity of the Word."

And again he says: "Using three successive testimonies, he wishes to show the eternity of the Word." And again he adds: "so that by saying 'In the beginning was the Word' he might show that the Word is in the Father in potency (for God is the beginning of all things that have come into being, 'from whom are all things'), and by saying 'and the Word was with God'

that the Word is with God in actuality (for 'all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being'), and by saying that the Word is God, that the Godhead is not to be divided, since the Word is in him and he in the Word; for he says, 'The Father is in me, and I am in the Father.'" With all these words Marcellus, abolishing the distinct existence of the only-begotten Son of God, calls the divine evangelist to witness for his own false belief, as though the evangelist knew him as nothing other than a word, now active and now at rest in God, and being nothing other than God himself.

And yet the great evangelist, who was also a theologian, though he mentioned the Word three times in the same passage, did not once call him the Word of God. For he did not say, "In the beginning was the Word of God," but without qualification, "In the beginning was the Word," leaving it to us to inquire what kind of Word this was. And again he said, "and the Word was with God," when he could have said, "and the Word of God was in God." Moreover, he said "and the Word was God," not "and the Word was of God," so that we should not suppose him to be some activity of God that signifies something or produces something.

Marcellus, supposing exactly this, has repeatedly defined him as the eternal Word of God, that is, unbegotten. He does not see that if he says the Word is other than God, there will be two eternal beings, the Word and God, and there will no longer be a single first principle. But if he says that the eternal is one, defining God as the same as the Word, he will openly profess the doctrine of Sabellius, introducing, just as Sabellius did, the one being as a Son-Father.

On his view, then, it will be the Father who was born and suffered, and it will be he himself who prays to himself and says that he was sent by himself, and who calls himself his own Son and only-begotten, not speaking the truth but lying in mockery. And what other doctrine could be more impious than this? But come, let us see what kind of Word the evangelist proclaims to us when he says: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

Now the term that denotes "word" (logos), as it is expressed in the Greek language, suggests many possible meanings. (1) For "logos" is the name given to the reason implanted in the rational soul, by which we are able to reason; (2) and besides this to another, the word that signifies something through the tongue and articulate voice; (3) and in a third sense, to the word composed in writing by the writer.

(4) Further, we are accustomed to call "logos" the seminal or vegetative principle, by which things that have not yet grown lie stored up in potency in the seeds, ready at any moment to come forth into the light in actuality. (5) And besides these, people are accustomed to use "logos" in yet another way for the systematic principle of some art or science, which comprehends all the propositions of that kind, as in medicine, architecture or geometry.

Since, then, the word "logos" presents various meanings, and the evangelist has said without qualification, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," we must apply our minds and recognize that the evangelist is here handing down to us a strange kind of Word, unlike those known to us. He speaks of "Word" without qualification, but he adds the strange and wonderful character of the power peculiar to him in the words "and the Word was God."

For do not suppose, he is saying, that this Word too belongs among relative things, like the word in the soul, or the word heard through the voice, or the principle in bodily seeds, or the principle that subsists in mathematical propositions. All of these, being relative, are conceived as existing in some other underlying substance. But God the Word does not need some other underlying thing in which he must come to be in order to subsist; he exists by himself, living and subsisting, because he is God. "For the Word was God."

And when you hear him called God, he is saying, do not suppose that he too is without beginning and unbegotten like his Father, but learn that this God the Word was "in the beginning." And what he posits as his beginning he makes clear next. He did not say, "and the Word was the God," with the addition of the article, lest he define him as the God who is over all; nor did he say "in God," lest he reduce him to a human likeness; but he said, "and the Word was with God."

For if he had said, "and the Word was in God," presenting it as an accident in a subject and as one thing in another, he would in effect have introduced a composite God, positing him as a substance without word and the word as an accident of that substance.

This is just what Marcellus supposes, and so he brings the Father and the Son together into one, calling the Father the substance and the Word in him the Son. He does not reckon that whoever grants this, positing God as without word, would fall into a godless and impious doctrine, accepting a God without reason, who has a word as an accident within him but is not himself Word.

Instead, one must confess that there is one divine being, ineffable, good, simple, incomposite, uniform, beyond the universe, who is God himself, Mind itself, Word itself, Wisdom itself, Light itself, Life itself, Beauty itself, Goodness itself, and whatever one might conceive that is better than these, or rather who is above all mind and beyond all thought and conception;

and that his only-begotten Son, as the image of the Father, sprung from him and in every way and in all respects most like the one who begot him, is himself also God and Mind and Word and Wisdom and Life and Light, and the image of the Beautiful and Good itself. He is not the Father himself but the only-begotten Son of the Father; nor is he the unbegotten and beginningless one himself, but the one sprung from him, who claims as his beginning the one who begot him.

But if Marcellus contradicts this and says that God and the Word in him are the same, defining God as incomposite and simple, then it is time for him to confess God as neither Father nor Son, and openly to put forward the Jew, or to bring in Sabellius, who says that Father and Son are the same. Thus on his view "In the beginning was the Word" would be equivalent to "In the beginning was God," and "and the Word was with God" would be equivalent to "and God was with God,"

and likewise the third clause would be the same as "and God was God"; and these, besides being incoherent, would also be utterly irrational. And how will "all things came into being through him" have any place, if there is only one subject? For he does not say that all things came into being by him or from him, but "through him." The preposition "through" signifies ministerial service, as the same evangelist shows a little further on when he says, "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." For just as the law, which was not human, nor Moses' own, but from God, enlisted Moses as minister and servant for its delivery to men, and for this reason it is said, "The law was given through Moses," so also "grace came through Jesus Christ," the Father having brought it about through Christ.

In the same way, then, it is said that "all things came into being through him," another having made them and he having served. So on Marcellus' view one would have to look for some other maker of the universe, who brought all things into being through the one whom the evangelist calls God. And who could this be? He would have nothing to say.

Since this is so, we must confess that the one whom the evangelist calls God is not the God who is over all, nor the Father himself, but his only-begotten Son: not an accident of the Father, nor existing in him as in a subject, nor one and the same with God, but truly a Son, living and subsisting, who was in the beginning and was with God and was God, through whom God creates all things.

So one might rightly, rephrasing it more clearly, say "In the beginning was the Son" instead of "In the beginning was the Word," and "and the Son was with the Father" instead of "and the Word was with God," and "and the Son was God" instead of "and the Word was God." In this way what follows next would also fit: "For all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being."

Fittingly, therefore, the divine evangelist said that he was "in the beginning," giving him a beginning, namely, clearly, his generation from the Father; for everything begotten of something has as its beginning the one who begot it. Yet he did not go on in the same way to say "and the Word was in God," but "the Word was with God," teaching that the one who was begotten and has the Father as his beginning is not somewhere far from the Father, nor cut off and standing at a distance from him, but is present to him and with him.

This is what was taught in Proverbs too, where he first said, "Before all the hills he begets me," and then added, "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him." So then the Word, that is, clearly, the only-begotten Son, was with his own Father, God, being with him and present with him always and at all times.

This the evangelist showed by saying, "and the Word was with God." And since we also needed to know what dignity he had, he necessarily joined to this, "and the Word was God." For how could he who was begotten of the one and only unbegotten God not be God? If, according to the Savior's teaching, "what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit," then it follows that what is begotten of God would be God. Therefore "the Word was God";

and God who makes and creates all things. This too the evangelist showed next, adding, "All things came into being through him." Now the law, which served as a tutor, introduced God through Moses in the account of the making of the world as the maker of the universe, and taught the first elements and introductory lessons of godliness, saying, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth," and what follows.
Through these words, as it tutored the people of the Jews, it urged them to consider the world as having come into being, so that they would not worship "the creature rather than the Creator."

But how God created all things, and through whom, Moses did not go on to teach those under him. Grace and truth, which came through Jesus Christ, proclaimed the mystery about which Moses had kept silent and began a newer and mystical teaching for the church of God, crying out openly to everyone, for all to hear: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and "All things came into being through him,

and without him not one thing came into being," and adding further to these, "What came into being in him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness," and what follows. Through these words it teaches about the Son of God and the distinctive qualities of the divine light and of the life in him, and how through him all the things Moses spoke of, and what lies even beyond them, were brought into being. But Marcellus, knowing none of this, is caught now Judaizing, now Sabellianizing:

like the Jew, he says that before the world was established nothing existed except God alone, whereas the church confesses that before the world was established the Father and the Son existed; and like Sabellius, he declares Son and Father to be one and the same, and presents him now as the internal word, now as the uttered word.

For even if he pretends not to accept these terms, he is nonetheless exposed by his saying at one time that the Word is within, in God, and at another that he proceeds from him by active energy, and by the ways in which he likens him to the human word. The divine evangelist, however, did not posit the one he calls God as a word in any of the senses listed, but as the only-begotten Son of God ought to be conceived: being Word inasmuch as he established all things by reason, and nothing that exists came into being without reason; and God and only-begotten inasmuch as he alone was truly the Son of the God over all, a Son truly genuine and beloved, made like his own Father in all things.

For this reason he was also truly light, inasmuch as he sheds an intellectual and rational radiance on souls made according to his image. That is why the evangelist says that he is the light not of all things but of human beings alone; for he said, "He was the light that enlightens every man coming into the world." So too he was truly life, inasmuch as he supplies to all living things the stream of his bounty. And for each conception of the divine powers in him you would find titles that truly represent him. For in every respect the Son of God was truth, as he himself shows when he says, "I am the truth."

But our new writer neither understands nor knows these things, nor does he even know that he is ignorant of the very things he boasts of knowing, namely how they came to be. Come, then, let us take up again and listen to how he likens the Word to the word in human beings, both the word in the mind and the uttered word, writing in this manner: "This, I think, is easy for sensible people to recognize even from a small and humble example from our own experience. For no one can separate a man's word from him in power and in hypostasis; the word is one and the same with the man, and is separated from him by nothing else than the mere activity of acting."

In these words he has used the image of the uttered word; and he uses that of the internal word where he says this: "For God did not need any other preparation for his construction, such as matter or anything else of a human sort, but only this preparation in his own mind. Since, then, it was impossible for God to think about the construction of heaven without word and without the wisdom that belongs to the word, he fittingly said, 'When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him.'"

Then, going on further, he presented the Word of God as at the same time internal as well, writing thus: "For who, either of the holy angels or of righteous men, was trustworthy enough to undo the punishment decreed for man by God's own mouth, except the Word himself, who was present with him and shared in shaping man, the one to whom the Father said, 'Let us make man'?"

After this he makes clear what kind of Word he is introducing, saying: "But suppose someone were to examine the divine act through an image, using a small human example from our own experience. A sculptor, a skilled man who wishes to fashion a statue, first considers its forms and features within himself, then works out what breadth and height would be fitting, and examines the proportion of the whole in each part. He prepares suitable material of bronze, prefigures the future statue in his own mind, and believes he sees it with his intellect; and he is aware that his word is working with him, the reason by which he reasons and by which he is accustomed to do everything (for nothing is fine that is not done by reason). Then, as he begins this work perceptible to the senses, he urges himself on as though addressing another, saying, 'Come, let us make, come, let us fashion a statue.' In the same way God, the Master of the universe, when making the living statue out of earth, urges on no one else but his own Word, saying, 'Let us make man.'" By these words he has plainly attributed to God both an internal word, by which one reasons, and an uttered word, by which one speaks, supposing that the Word in God is of the same kind as ours.

Now since all these statements amount to denials of the Son of God, there is no need to work them over further. But I think it fitting to ask this much: if there was one God and nothing else, neither Father nor Son, why did Scripture tell lies with such names? And why does Marcellus himself play the hypocrite, calling the Word, which is not a son, a Son? And since he has used the word in human beings as an example, it must be said that not every human being has a son, though every human being is rational and possesses the word innate in himself.

So a son is something other than a word. If, then, he says that God has a word in himself and nothing else, by which he thought and by which he conversed with himself, saying, "Let us make man," why does he speak of a Son for no reason? Why does he make a pretense of belonging to the church? And why, though he does not believe in the Son of God, does he pretend to believe, putting on a show by calling the Word in God a Son, when his own example clearly teaches that the word innate in the soul is far different from a son who is begotten of someone and subsists by himself, living and active?
"But it is not I," he will probably say, "but the divine evangelist who called him Word; so it follows that we too should agree with him." Yes, I say so too.

Only I think we ought to understand the term in no other way than by learning once more from the evangelist himself, who teaches what kind of Word he meant. And he showed clearly what sort of Word this was by adding next, "and the Word was God." Though he could have said, "and the Word was the God," with the addition of the article, if he had thought that the Father and the Son were one and the same and that the Word himself was the God over all, he did not write the scripture that way.

For if he had been making Scripture agree with Marcellus' way of thinking, he should have said either "and the Word was of God" or "the Word was the God," with the article. As it is, he shows that the Word himself is also God, like the God with whom he was. For having first said, "and the Word was with God," he goes on to say, "and the Word was God," all but teaching us more plainly, first, to regard as God the one who is beyond the universe, the very Father of the Word, with whom the Word was; and then, after him, not to be unaware that his Word too, the only-begotten Son, was not himself the God over all, but that he too was God.

For the conjunction "and" joins the Son's divinity to the Father. That is why he says, "and the Word was God," so that we may see as God the God over all, with whom the Word was. And understand the Word himself as God, as the image of God; and an image not as in lifeless matter, but as in a living Son, made most exactly like the archetypal divinity of the Father.

And since Marcellus saw fit to compare the Word of God with the human word, how much better, we shall say, it would have been, if he was going to use the human word as an image, to use this example instead and say that the father of our word is the mind, which is something other than the word. For no human being has ever known what the mind is or what kind of thing it is in its essence; like a king seated within its secret chambers, it deliberates on what is to be done. But the word that comes from it, born as from a father out of the innermost recesses, becomes known to everyone outside.
Others then share in the benefit of the word, but the hidden and invisible mind, the father of the word, no one has ever seen.

In the same way, or rather in a way beyond every image and example, the perfect Word of God, the King of all, is not composed, like the uttered word of human beings, of syllables, verbs and nouns. As the only-begotten Son of God, living and subsisting, he goes forth from the Father's divinity and kingdom and waters the whole world with the bounties that come from him, flooding all created things with a share in life and word and wisdom and light and every good thing. Meanwhile the Father and God of the universe is beyond, incomprehensible and uncontainable to all, like the hidden and invisible mind, which is why he is also said to "dwell in unapproachable light."

The Father, then, would be unapproachable and uncontainable to all, while the Son is nearer to all, since he governs all things at the Father's command (which is why it is said not of the Father but of the Son, "He was in the world, and the world came into being through him"). The one was beyond the universe and above all things, "dwelling in unapproachable light," while the other pervades all things and is in all things by his caring providence; so it is only in this respect that the image of the human word fits him. But now that we have demonstrated these things, some lover of learning will likely ask:

Why did the evangelist, at the beginning of his writing, proclaim the only-begotten Son of God as "Word"? To this we shall say: because of the prophecies about him that had long been hidden. For with each prophet it is said, "the word of the Lord which came" – to Isaiah, for example – and "the beginning of the word of the Lord in Hosea," and "the word of the Lord which came to Joel," and "the word of the Lord came to Jonah,"

and likewise to Micah, and in the same way to the rest of the prophets. With each prophet the word "came" was added, because the divine scripture notes precisely and necessarily that the Word did not dwell in any of the prophets but came to each one. He approached each as far as that prophet's capacity could receive him, and supplied each one's soul with the fitting spirit from himself. Now the evangelist was about to proclaim the spiritual dispensation of the Word, so it is fitting that he does not teach that the Word came to someone else, as with those of old. He teaches that the Word himself took on flesh and became man. Then, since he was going to proclaim to everyone the Word's saving entry among humankind, and was about to say next, "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us," he necessarily runs back to the beginning. He shows who this Word was, so recently made flesh, and what kind of being he was,

and he speaks of him as God, proclaiming at once the knowledge of him and his divine appearance to humankind. Those of old had already learned from the divine readings about the Word that came to each prophet. So John himself proclaims the Word's more divine and exceptional beginning, which none of the prophets had ever revealed to people so plainly and without a veil.

Therefore, with a loud voice, he handed on to all the mystery about the Word that had been hidden and secret, crying out: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being."

"For if," he says, "you were schooled by the earlier divine scriptures and learned long ago that the word of the Lord came to this prophet, and likewise came to another, and again to yet another, it is now necessary to proclaim to all, not how he came, but how he was in the beginning. It must be proclaimed that he was God, that all things came into being through him, and that this very God the Word, through whom are all things, became flesh and dwelt among us through the Father's love for humankind."

This is the good news that John, the great disciple and apostle of Christ, proclaimed, teaching all people the new and fresh mysteries of the Savior. He did not teach that God was rational, nor that God thought within himself and conversed with himself when he said, "Let us make man," nor that he used words that command what is to be done. For anyone who denies the Son of God might say such things.

This is just what Marcellus does. He flees to the old scripture as if to a hiding place, and he tries to collect the commands given to the infant Jewish people about not worshiping idols but knowing and worshiping one God alone. There, indeed, the teaching about the one God served him well. That teaching had been given usefully at that time, and at the right moment, to Jews who were worshiping idols. So, having taken refuge there and fenced himself in with Jewish hardness of heart as if inside a fortress, he put forward his denial of the Son of God.

Listen, then, to the words he uses. He writes as follows, word for word: "Whom, then, does Asterius think it is who says, 'I am he who is'? The Son or the Father? For Asterius looks to the human flesh that the Word of God assumed and, imagining things in this way because of it, has said that there are two hypostases, of Father and of Son. He thus separates the Son of God from the Father as one might separate a son of man from his natural father."

And he goes on: "If, then, he says that the Father, separating himself from the Son, said these things to Moses, he will be confessing that the Son is not God. For how can the one who says 'I am he who is' not also acknowledge that he calls himself 'he who is' in contrast to what is not? But if he claims that it is the Son, divided in hypostasis, who says this 'I am he who is,' he will in turn be thought to say the same about the Father. Both of these are impious."

And again, trying to show that the Father and the Son are one, he writes thus: "For he himself confesses, saying, 'The Father is in me and I am in the Father.' That he did not say this casually or without purpose is clear also from another apostolic saying. Having said, 'One Lord, one faith, one baptism,' the apostle said, 'One God and Father, who is over all and through all and in all.' You see that even here he does not depart from that agreement. Here too he expresses the same thing. For having said 'one Lord,' he then said 'one God.' So whenever he mentions the one Lord he includes the Father as well, and whenever he speaks of the Father he bears witness that the Word of God is not outside him."
After saying this, Marcellus goes on to collect more texts from the Old Testament to prove that God has no Son.

Thus, asserting that God is an indivisible Monad, he presented the same one as Father and the same one as Son, writing in this way: "What then? If we attend to the Spirit and yet do not hold that the Monad is indivisible in power, shall we not sin? For the Word clearly teaches us, 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.'

"He proclaims the same thing through the Gospel according to Mark as well. A certain scribe came to him and asked which was the first of the commandments, and he answered him: 'First of all: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your soul and with all your strength. This is the first. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
"There is no other commandment greater than these.' And the scribe said to him, 'Well said, Teacher; you have truly said that God is one and there is none besides him.'

"The scribe, who appears to have learned piety through the law, clearly praises the Savior's saying 'Hear, O Israel' when the Savior says, 'The Lord your God is one.' He even confirms with an oath that it was rightly said, for he says, 'Truly you have said that God is one and there is no other besides him.' Yet those who boast that they know the mysteries of the new covenant want to fabricate even a second God, separated from the Father in hypostasis and in power."

To this he adds the following, arguing that God is one and that there is no Son: "That the divine scripture knows how to call the Monad Lord and God has already become clear from what was said earlier, where God spoke to his servant Moses: 'And God said again to Moses: Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' You see how, showing us one person here, he calls the same one Lord and God.

"And again scripture likewise says: 'And the Lord spoke all these words, saying: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods besides me.' You hear how through the pronoun he declares that there is only one God.

"And again, a little later, he says, 'I am the Lord your God,' declaring that he himself is Lord and God. And what do we learn through another scripture? 'And you shall know today,' it says, 'and not be turned aside in your mind, that the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on the earth below, and there is none besides him.' And again in the same Deuteronomy it says, 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.'

"And again in the same book: 'See, see that I am, and there is no God besides me; I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike and I will heal.' How, then, did Asterius, who pretends to follow the holy scriptures simply and with reverent fear, not know this passage? It says, 'The Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on the earth below, and there is no other besides him,' declaring that he is one and that besides him there is no other."

And after other matters he adds to this again, saying: "How, then, will the holy prophet Jeremiah not plainly refute him as one who teaches a different doctrine? For when he prophesied to us about the Savior, he spoke thus: 'This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. After this he was seen on earth and lived among men.'"

And again he adds: "But it seems that the Father is in the Word, even if Asterius and those who think as he does do not think so. For the inspired prophet Isaiah thought so, who says through the Holy Spirit: 'And they shall worship you, and in you they shall pray, for God is in you, and there is no other besides you. For you are God.' Do you see how he tears out by the root the cunning mischief of those who teach a different doctrine?"

And again he adds: "And if you also wish to hear another prophecy of the same prophet confirming one God to us: 'I, God, am first,' he says, 'and for the things to come, I am.' The word 'I' points to a single person. Indeed, the two words signify one person to us. Having said 'I,' he adds 'am' as well, so that through the two parts of speech, pronoun and verb, the oneness of the Godhead is attested.

"And if he needs yet another testimony, I will again present to him the same prophet saying: 'I am first and I am after these things, and besides me there is no God.' Asterius thinks that the Son is divided from the Father in hypostasis, as a son of man is, because he takes offense at the human flesh that the Son took on for our sake. If so, let him show us who it is that says these things.

"For here too the saying is spoken by one person. Who, then, is it that says, 'There is no God besides me'? And let him also hear another prophecy, which says, 'There is no one righteous and a savior besides me.' If he thinks there are two gods, he must confess that the other is neither righteous nor a savior. And if he is neither righteous nor a savior, how can he still be God? For the prophet declares that one alone is righteous and savior. And again he says, 'Before me there was no other, and after me there shall be none; I am God, and there shall be no one who saves apart from me.'

"And if he wishes to hear yet another prophetic saying, perhaps spoken against him and those who hold similar views about the Godhead, let him hear Isaiah himself saying, 'Repent, you who go astray; turn back in your heart, and remember the former things from of old, that I am the God, and there is none besides me.'

"He did not say, 'I am God,' without the article. By adding the article he clearly shows that he is the one God. And what of Hosea the prophet? Does he not also bear witness to the same when he says, 'I brought you up out of Egypt, and you shall know no God besides me, and there is no one who saves apart from me'? And again Malachi says, 'Did not one God

"create you? Is there not one Father of you all?' But perhaps Asterius will say that David said nothing about this, even though, apart from Moses, he was the most ancient of the prophets. He may say that he is therefore in doubt whether or not one ought to think there are two gods divided in hypostasis. So that he may not say this, I think it fitting to show him that David too says the same as the holy men mentioned before: 'Hear, my people,' he says, 'and I will speak to you; Israel, and I will testify to you. If you hear me, there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god.
"For I am the Lord your God.' He points to himself and says 'I am.' Is it not clear that he is saying there is only one God, that is, himself?"

Marcellus heaped up all these texts, and still more besides, to deny the Son of God. Through lack of understanding he failed to consider that such teaching was given to them because of the hardness of heart of the Jewish people. It was not possible for the Holy Spirit, speaking through the prophets of God, to hand over the complete word of piety to people whose minds were immature.

So it was that he laid down laws for them about offering sacrifices, circumcision of the body, keeping the Sabbath, abstaining from certain foods, purifications of the body and bodily blessings. He even gave them promises of a land flowing with milk and honey, but not of the kingdom of heaven. Our Savior and Lord was asked why, when Moses had commanded that any man who wished could give his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away, he himself ordered the opposite. He gave an explanation that applies generally: "Moses wrote this for you because of your hardness of heart; but from the beginning it was not so."

He would have said the same if someone had asked why Moses and the prophets after him, while urging the people to worship one God, did not teach them the knowledge of the Son. Those who were continually being led away into the error of many gods could not receive the grace of the gospel. Therefore, because of their hardness of heart, the prophets gave them the teaching about one God. For the time being, they schooled the people by turning them away from the belief that there are many gods and by leading them toward acceptance of the one.

Because the people of Moses' time were immature in understanding, the teaching he handed on to them was so incomplete that he made no mention of the creation of angels in his account of the making of the world. Yet the prophets after him mentioned not only angels but also divine powers and holy spirits, the ministers of God above the heavens. Daniel taught about them, saying, "A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him."

But Moses passed over all these in silence. He was not ignorant of them; through the divine Spirit he had already received precise knowledge of them all. Nevertheless, in his account of creation he made no mention of them at all as beings made by God.

One could give no other reason for this than the hardness of heart of the people, just as the Savior himself taught. And you could learn from the readings of the new covenant that the order of the universe contains countless other things that are not mentioned at all in the writings of Moses. He did not mention principalities, or authorities, or world rulers, or the spiritual forces of wickedness, against which, the divine apostle says, our struggle is set.

What then? Since accounts of these things cannot be clearly found either in Moses or in the other prophets, must we disbelieve the apostle? The same apostle also mentions the ranks of higher beings when he says that Christ is seated at the right hand of God, far above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come,

and he names thrones and dominions and principalities and authorities when he says, "For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or authorities." Is it, then, not right to accept these things, because neither Moses nor the other prophets had spoken of them beforehand? Or shall we not say the same about these things too, that the stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart and ears, were unable to believe accounts of them? The prophets of God did not reveal to them anything even about the Jerusalem above. Paul, however, made the account of it plain to the church of Christ as well, crying out, "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother," and, "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven."
Let Marcellus answer this: can he produce teaching about these things from the old writings?

And if he cannot find any, let him give the reason why the prophets of God kept silent about all these things, and about countless others like them. The same apostle prayed to God on our behalf about these things, that we might be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and depth and height, and to know the love of God that surpasses knowledge.

And our Savior himself revealed a great many mysteries to his disciples, sometimes through parables and sometimes in private. They concerned the kingdom of heaven, the end of all things and the promises. To his disciples he said, "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of God." One would not find anything equal to these in Moses or in the other prophets.

What then? These things were not handed down to the Jewish people but were kept for the church of Christ until the proper time. Should we on that account reject the grace given to us, or should we rather give greater thanks to him who counted us worthy of such great knowledge? In the same way, then, it is fitting to receive the teachings about the Son from his own new covenant. We should not be at all surprised if the men of God did not reveal the knowledge of him to a hard-hearted people, but stored up the word about him for the right time.

For at that time it did not seem suitable to hand over the mystery of the Father and the Son to men who were being dragged into the error of many gods. The prophets did not reveal to them even the accounts of the lower powers, so that this would not become a pretext for them to fall into the polytheism of the Greeks, who had fashioned their god as "father of men and gods."

Therefore the Word, holding them back from such error, proclaimed the one God, yet did not deny that this same God is Father. It taught them to worship the true God and urged them to acknowledge no one besides him, yet did not deny that he is Father. And although it called him Lord and God and righteous and Savior, it did not rule out regarding him also as Father of his only-begotten and beloved Son. So whether it is the Father who says "I am he who is" or the Son,

the statement would be true either way. For the Father would be "he who is," since he alone is God over all and through all and in all, as the divine apostle taught. And the Son too would speak truly when he bears the title "he who is," since he alone is the only-begotten Son of him who is. Moreover, since he is the image of the invisible God, he would be God's image in precisely this respect: that God alone was "he who is." Therefore the Son too would bear the title "he who is," since he too, like the Father, is proclaimed God and Lord throughout the whole of divinely inspired scripture.

This can also be learned from the oracle given to Moses. Scripture says: "And God spoke to Moses and said to him, I am the Lord; and I appeared to Abraham and to Isaac and to Jacob, being their God." You see how he said that he had appeared to the fathers. And when he appeared, Scripture again testifies, saying: "And the Lord God appeared to Abraham by the oak of Mamre, as he sat at the door." And how did he appear, if not in human form? And whom ought we to believe this was, if not the Son of God? This is just what he himself showed in the Gospels, when he said to the Jews: "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; and he saw it and was glad."

And when they marveled at this saying, he added, "Before Abraham came to be, I am," showing his own pre-existence most clearly. What, then, does the passage establish, if not that the Son of God himself is the one who gave the oracle to Moses and said, "I am he who is"? For he himself taught that he had appeared to Abraham. And how he himself was "he who is" has already been explained.

The great apostle Paul, too, knows that the Son of God was the mediator of the law given through Moses, when he teaches: "The law was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one." So the one who gave the oracle to Moses was the mediator, who from that time was mediating for the salvation of human beings, even before he took on flesh.

That this is Jesus Christ the same apostle showed when he said: "There is one God, and one mediator also between God and men, the man Jesus Christ." So whether the words "I am he who is" were spoken to Moses in the Son's own person, or whether it was the Father who uttered this voice through him, the statement would be true either way.

So let Marcellus not be perplexed, though he uses a syllogism he thinks inescapable, in which he says: "Whom then does Asterius think is the one who says 'I am he who is,' the Son or the Father?" He then goes on to conclude that if the Father were "he who is," the Son would no longer be God, since he calls himself "he who is" in contrast to what is not. But if Asterius were to say that it is the Son, divided off by his own hypostasis, who says "I am he who is," then he will in turn be thought to be saying the same thing about the Father; and each of these is impious.

But in saying this, Marcellus himself has fallen into both absurdities, defining one as "he who is" and denying the other. Which one that is, he himself would know. For either he will grant the Father and deny the Son, or he will accept the Son alone and set aside the Father; or rather, he will be shown to know neither Father nor Son, since he grants only one and removes the other from the scene. And even if he hears God saying, "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery;

you shall have no other gods besides me," let him not be troubled in soul here either, but let him listen also to the words joined to them.
