For having said, "You shall have no other gods besides me," he went on: "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not bow down to them nor serve them; for I am the Lord your God, a jealous Lord."

You see how he strictly commanded them not to be carried off along with the polytheistic error of the nations, but to know him alone as God and Lord. And who was this? The Son, who has in himself the image of the Father, and who on his authority gave these commands to those afflicted with idolatry. For just as "all things came into being through him," the Father having established through the Savior the substance of all things that have come into being, so too it was the Father himself who handed on to human beings the knowledge of himself and piety toward himself through the Son as mediator.
The apostle taught this in so many words when writing to the Galatians, where he said: "The law was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one."

And even if he says, "See, see that I am, and there is no God besides me," again it was the Father saying this through the Son, as through an image and mediator. For when the prophet Isaiah says, "I have begotten sons and raised them up," and again, "But Israel has not known me, and the people has not understood me," and again, "I commanded all the stars, and with my hand I established the heaven," and all other such things, we will not say that Isaiah is saying these things, but God who speaks in him, through him. If so, would it not also be fitting, in the case of the only-begotten Son of God, that the Father should have had to solemnly declare these things through him to those who needed such commands? And these people were idolaters, as the same Scripture teaches when it says: "And the Lord said: Where are their gods, in whom they trusted? whose fat of their sacrifices you ate, and you drank the wine of their libations; let them rise up and help you, and let them be your protectors." For it is to these words that "See, see that I am, and there is no God besides me" is joined.

So even if, crying out through the prophet ten thousand times, he says, "Besides me there is no God," and "Besides me there is none righteous and a Savior," and "You shall know no God besides me, and there is none who saves besides me," and all the other things akin to these that are found in the rest of the prophets, it was God who even then was "in Christ reconciling the world to himself." And it was the Father himself who uttered these things to human beings through the only-begotten Son, as through an interpreter. This too the Son himself handed down in the Gospels, teaching that one God alone is to be known, when he said: "And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent."

He, then, was the true God, the one and only, and there is no other besides him; and he enjoined these things, not only through the prophets but through his own Son, on the nation of the Jews, which at that time was given to idolatry. So, for instance, Isaiah (or rather God through him), having said, "Besides me there is no God. Who is like me?" and next, "You are witnesses whether there is a God besides me," went on: "And there were none then. Those who mold and those who carve are all vain, doing what they themselves desire."

Throughout his whole prophecy you will find lifeless wooden idols being struck down, and likewise in each of the prophets you will find the one God proclaimed in order to turn people away from polytheistic error. So we too, in our dialogues with superstitious Greeks, are accustomed to hold back the teaching about Christ for the right moment, and meanwhile to offer them refutations of idolatrous error and to establish by demonstrative arguments that God is one.

Let Marcellus learn, then, if even now, after growing old in the episcopate of Christ's church, he has not yet learned it, that knowledge of the hidden mystery concerning the Son of God was in no way suited to the ancient people, who were prone to slip into idolatry, and that the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations was reserved by his grace for his church alone, the mystery in which the doctrine of the holy Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, was contained.

But he, having gathered as many passages as even a Jewish teacher might cite when preaching on circumcision in a Jewish synagogue, prides himself on putting them forward to the disciples of Christ, not realizing that a carnal Jew could say more than he does. In these things he boasts, yet he is not ashamed to distort the true teachings about the divinity of our Savior.

For instance, he does not understand the words of the divine apostle, who taught in various ways that the Son is the image of God, in the passages of his that I have set out; whereas from them he ought to understand that the church of God does not proclaim two Gods. For it does not introduce two unbegotten beings, nor two without beginning, as we have often said, nor two essences set side by side against each other with equal honor, and therefore not two Gods either. Rather, it teaches one first principle and God, and that this same one is the Father of the only-begotten and beloved Son, and likewise one "image of the invisible God," which is the same as his only-begotten and beloved Son. And even if the apostle, speaking of the Father as God, says, "the blessed and only Sovereign," and again, "who alone has immortality,

dwelling in unapproachable light," and again, "To the King of the ages, incorruptible, invisible, the only God," and again, "to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory forever. Amen"; and even if still more than these is said in praise of the one God over all, we must understand that the only-begotten Son of God is the image of all these things too, an image formed not in lifeless matter but in a living Son. And even if the Savior himself teaches that the Father is the only true God, saying, "that they may know you, the only true God," we must still not hesitate to confess that he too is true God, as possessing this also in the manner of an image, so that the addition "only" may belong to the Father alone, as the archetype of the image.

At any rate, the inspired Paul taught most clearly that the Son is the image and radiance of the Father and is in the form of God, as was shown above. Now when there is one Father subsisting and one Son born of the Father, no one in his right mind would say that there are two fathers or two sons. And when one emperor rules and his image is displayed everywhere on earth, no one of sound mind would say that there are two rulers, but one, who is honored also through his image. In the same way (as we have often said), the church of God too, having received the tradition of worshiping one God, continues to worship that same God also through the Son, as through an image.

Not understanding this, Marcellus declared that the image of the invisible God is the flesh of the Savior, which the apostle called "the form of a slave," without considering that all human beings too have been given the same form as the Savior's flesh. He insists that the body the Savior assumed is the image of the unbegotten, ineffable, paternal Godhead, but denies that the only-begotten Son of God, through whom all things were established ("for all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being"), is the image of God, saying in these very syllables: "It is therefore evident that before the assumption of our body the Word in himself was not the image of the invisible God." You see how badly he twists the apostle's meaning.

In this way, while the evangelist John was proclaiming as good news and unveiling the mystery that had been known in a hidden way in Moses and the rest of the prophets, and was announcing with a loud cry, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

All things came into being through him," and was bearing witness that "he was the light that enlightens every human being coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him," and was clearly showing his sonship by saying of the Father, "No one has ever seen God," and of the Son, "The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known,"

this marvelous teacher of the words of Christ gathers from divine Scripture the commandments of God and the words that prescribe what is to be done, and defines the Word who was in the beginning as something of that sort. Listen to how he tries to establish this, writing in this way: * * * * * "…while those who teach them seem ashamed, as it were, to mention the Word, whom all the divine Scriptures proclaim in this way. For David says of him, 'By the word of the Lord the heavens were established,' and again, 'He sent his word and healed them.' And Solomon: 'The wicked will seek me and will not find me; for they hated wisdom and did not choose the word of the Lord.' And Isaiah: 'Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.' And again Jeremiah: 'The wise,' he says, 'were put to shame and dismayed and caught, because they rejected the word of the Lord.'

"And the prophet Hosea said, 'They hated the one who reproves in the gates, and they abhorred the holy word.' Likewise Micah, also making mention of the Word, said, 'Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.'" Having gathered these and similar passages, he thinks he is strengthening his own opinion by them.

But see how he has jumbled together the testimonies from divine Scripture and lumped together both the Word of God who is sent forth, the one who saves and heals, and the word that prescribes what is to be done. For in "They hated the one who reproves in the gates, and they abhorred the holy word," what word does it assume, if not surely the word that prescribes holy and righteous deeds? He would rather confess anything than the Son of God, as though ashamed to mention the Son. For we know that the Son of God is Son in the most proper sense and truly the only-begotten of God; and we know precisely that he is also Word, not like the word found among human beings, but such as it befits us to conceive the Word of God to be: living, subsisting, and Son. But Marcellus, who brings in a word that conveys meaning and prescribes what is to be done, naturally hesitated to confess the Son, whom in very deed he denied.

Then too he does not notice that he is contradicting himself in what he writes. For elsewhere he insists that none of the former people knew about the Word, because it was a hidden mystery. He writes this in these very words: "For what else was the hidden mystery but that concerning the Word? This mystery was formerly so hidden in God that none of the former people knew clearly about the Word, but we now enjoy the riches of the glory and of the hidden mystery." And again he adds: "But the holy apostle and disciple of the Lord, John, teaching clearly and expressly at the beginning of the Gospel, as of something formerly unknown among human beings, and naming him the Word of the Almighty, spoke thus: 'In the beginning was the Word.'" In these passages, then, he defines the hidden mystery as the fact that God has a Word; yet in the prophetic sayings just cited he maintains that all the divine Scriptures proclaim what concerns him, and he collects a great many testimonies about the Word of God.

So he was not unknown to the former people after all, for they all knew such words, having the prophetic oracles on their lips and in their memory. But this Christian holds up the Jewish scribe to us, without heeding the Savior when he says, "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!" He admires the scribe for affirming on oath that "God is one and there is no other besides him," not knowing that "even the demons believe, and shudder."

Note how he gathers from the prophetic Scriptures themselves the passages about the word that teaches what is to be done, a word that even the children of the Jews will acknowledge they know, since they received it before we did. Indeed, not even Sabellius himself was ignorant of such a word.

How, then, in the passages of his that I have cited, could he attack the Jews and Sabellius and say that they did not know the Word? And since he himself declared earlier that no one could know God or recognize his Word unless the Word had taken on the image of the invisible God, that is, the flesh, as he himself said

(for he insisted that God and his Word are known only through the image, saying that the flesh is the image), we must point out, from what has been set forth, that even without the coming in the flesh all the Jews knew precisely the word of God and the words in the prophetic Scriptures that prescribe holy works, since they studied them from their earliest years; and they confessed God as the maker and creator of all things, just as the scribe did when he affirmed this on oath.

So much, then, by way of demonstrating that the man is a Sabellian. It is now time to go on to the distorted interpretations of the divine Scriptures that he has produced, so that everyone who holds the man in honor may learn that he has strayed not only from the right faith but also from a sound reading and understanding of the divinely inspired Scriptures.

Now the great evangelist John proclaimed the divinity of our Savior in various ways, in the manner already described; and how Marcellus denied it and ran aground on Jewish unbelief has been made clear by what has been said. That he also perversely misinterpreted the acknowledged and clear teachings about our Savior you could learn from a great many other expositions of his, but above all from the following. In the Proverbs of Solomon, Wisdom is introduced speaking in her own person and relating these things about herself: "I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling,

and I have called upon knowledge and understanding. The fear of the Lord hates wickedness, insolence and arrogance, and the ways of the wicked; and I have hated the perverse ways of evil people. Counsel and safety are mine; I am understanding, and strength is mine.

Through me kings reign, and rulers decree righteousness; through me great men are made great, and through me tyrants rule the earth. I love those who love me, and those who seek me will find me. Wealth and glory are mine, and abundant possessions, and righteousness.

It is better to enjoy my fruit than gold and precious stone, and my produce is better than choice silver. I walk in the ways of righteousness, and I go about in the midst of the paths of justice, so that I may give substance as their portion to those who love me and fill their treasuries with good things. If I declare to you the things that happen day by day, I will remember to recount the things of old.

The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works; before the age he established me, in the beginning, before he made the earth, before he made the depths, before the springs of water came forth, before the mountains were settled, and before all the hills he begets me. The Lord made lands, both uninhabited regions and the inhabited heights of the world beneath the heavens. When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him, when he was marking out his throne upon the winds; when he was making the clouds above strong, and setting the springs beneath heaven securely, and making the foundations of the earth strong, I was beside him, setting things in order. I was the one in whom he delighted daily, and I rejoiced before his face at all times, when he rejoiced at having completed the world, and rejoiced among the children of men."

This is what Wisdom says about herself in Proverbs. I have deliberately set out the whole passage, as I had to, in order to show that it is one and the same person [?] which Marcellus transferred to the Savior's flesh who says these things, with no change of speaker anywhere in between. So it is shown that it is Wisdom who teaches these things about herself. And here we must first notice that she is called simply "Wisdom." For she says, "I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling," and it is not said, "the Wisdom of God." In the evangelist, "In the beginning was the Word" was written without qualification, and again "the Word was with God," and it was not said "the Word of God," so that no one would think he was spoken of as something relative, or as an attribute in God, but as subsisting and living. That is why he adds, "and the Word was God," not saying, "and the Word was God's." In the same way, then, with Wisdom too.

For God the Word and Wisdom were one and the same. That is why in Proverbs she is named without qualification, both in the passages quoted above and also in those where it is said in this manner: "Blessed is the man who has found wisdom"; and "God founded the earth by wisdom"; and "Say that wisdom is your sister"; and "Proclaim wisdom, so that understanding may follow you"; and "For wisdom is better than precious stones";

and "Wisdom has built herself a house, and has set up seven pillars"; and all the other passages like these that occur in the same book. In none of them is she called "the Wisdom of God," but simply "Wisdom," so that we should not suppose her to be some attribute belonging to God, as knowledge is in a knowledgeable man, but a subsisting and living Wisdom, the same as the Son of God.

But if anyone supposes that the Wisdom spoken of here is a wise disposition in God, by virtue of which we think of God as wise, let him listen to Scripture saying, "Say that wisdom is your sister." Who would be so mad as to suppose that the God over all, and the wise disposition in him, is called the sister of those among men who do what is right?

But if you take the saying as referring to the Christ of God (for "Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God"), nothing will stand in the way of the sense, since in the abundance of his love for mankind he does not refuse even to be our brother. If, on the other hand, God and the Wisdom introduced in Proverbs were one and the same, she being a wise disposition conceived of in him by virtue of which God is wise, what prevented "God" from being written instead of "Wisdom"? Then "Wisdom has built herself a house, and has set up seven pillars," and what is joined to it, would have been said in place of "God has built himself a house," and so on; and again,
"Say that wisdom is your sister" would have been said in place of "Say that God is your brother." But you see how such language jars on the ear, lacking all harmony.

If, however, you take these sayings as referring to the Son (for he was Wisdom), everything will flow smoothly for you, with no impious notion standing in the way; and the apostle Paul bears witness as well, who in a clear voice called our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ Wisdom, saying, "Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God."

With this established in some such way, it follows that, together with everything set out before, the words "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works" were also spoken by the same person. And if he says that he was created, he would not be saying this as one who passed from non-being into being, nor as one who, like the rest of creatures, himself came into existence out of nothing, as some have wrongly supposed, but as one who subsists and lives, and who was before and existed prior to the formation of the whole world, and who was appointed by the Lord, his own Father, to rule over all things. For "created" is said here in place of "appointed" or "established."

Indeed, the apostle explicitly called the rulers and governors among men a "creation" when he said, "Submit yourselves to every human creation for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him."

And the prophet who said, "Prepare to call upon your God, Israel. For behold, I am he who makes the thunder firm, and creates spirit, and announces his Christ to men," and also the verse "Let this be written for another generation, and the people that is being created will praise the Lord," did not use "creating" of something that came into being out of non-existence. For God did not create the Spirit at the moment when he proclaimed his Christ to all men through him; "there is nothing new under the sun."

Rather, the Spirit was, and existed beforehand, but was sent at the time when the apostles were gathered together, when there came a sound from heaven like thunder, "as of a rushing violent wind," and "they were filled with the Holy Spirit," and so proclaimed the Christ of God to all men, in accordance with the prophecy that said, "For behold, I am he who makes the thunder firm, and creates spirit, and announces his Christ to men." Here "creates" is said in place of "sends down" or "appoints," while the thunder signifies, in a figurative way, the proclamation of the gospel. And the one who says, "Create in me a clean heart, O God," did not say this as one who had no heart; he was praying that his mind might be made clean.

In the same way it is said, "that he might create the two into one new man," in place of "bring together." Consider whether "Put on the new man, created according to God" is not of the same kind, and "So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation," and all the other expressions of this sort one might find by searching the divinely inspired Scripture. So do not be surprised if in "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways" the word "created" is used metaphorically in place of "established" or "appointed to rule." For in the Gospels too, when our Savior says, "I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants," we do not say that the Savior means the confession of sins (in the sense in which it is said elsewhere, "Confess your sins to one another"), but thanksgiving for the infants, "I confess" being said in place of "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth."

Anyone who searched at leisure could find countless things throughout the whole of divine Scripture that are said metaphorically, others that carry many meanings, and still others that are predicated equivocally of different things. It would take long to go through them, and this is not the occasion.

So here too, "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works" is said in place of "He appointed me to rule over his works." That is why it does not say simply "He created me," but adds "the beginning of his ways for his works."

The Hebrew wording shows this most clearly. Anyone who examined closely the true sense of the divinely inspired Scripture would find that the Hebrew reading does not contain "he created me," and that is why none of the other translators used this word either. Aquila, for example, said, "The Lord acquired me as the chief of his ways"; Symmachus, "The Lord acquired me as the beginning of his ways"; and Theodotion, "The Lord acquired me as the beginning of his way."

And this rendering would make good sense. For he himself was the chief, the summing-up, of the formation and salvation of all things that have come into being, visible and invisible. The Father begot him as only-begotten Son, and having begotten him appointed him Savior of all, summing up in him and through him the ordering of the universe, as the divine apostle taught when he said, "to sum up all things in Christ, things in the heavens and things on earth." Thus not only were all things constituted through him, coming forth from non-being into being, but he also took on himself the providential care of the government of all things, since he is Word and Wisdom and Life and the fullness of everything fine and good, so that through him all things are steered and preserved.
He himself made this plain in the sayings quoted above, where he said, "By me kings reign, and princes decree justice; by me great men are made great, and by me sovereigns rule the earth."

All things, then, are governed by the ineffable principles of the universal wisdom and providence of the Son of God. This is what he taught in the passages set out above. He urged men to cling to him, saying, "I love those who love me, and those who seek me will find me," and he turned them away from the opposite road by adding, "I have hated the crooked ways of the wicked."

Having set out these things and others like them, the Son of God (for he was Wisdom) next hands on the mystical knowledge about himself to those who have already benefited from them, saying, "If I declare to you the things that happen day by day, I will remember to recount the things from of old."

"For if I am going to teach," he says, "what I do each day, I must also recall my works from the beginning of all the ages, and show that the Father who begot me appointed me for this purpose: to rule over all things, and to lead the way in his ways and in the works he has made through me." That is why he goes on, fittingly, to say, "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works," or, according to the rendering given above, "The Lord acquired me."

For the only-begotten Son was God's great possession: insofar as he was begotten from him, being his Son, and insofar as he was established as a common benefit and source of salvation for all, he both is and is called the Father's greatest and most precious possession. Nothing could be a more precious possession to a father than a son. Hence, when Adam, the first-formed, gained the first son among mankind, it was said of him too, "I have acquired a man through God," where the Hebrew word in place of "I have acquired" is kanithi;

while "he acquired" is pronounced kana among the Hebrews. So it is said of Abraham, "the field which Abraham acquired," where the Hebrew has kana; and the same word stands in the Hebrew in "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works." Since here too the word kana stands, all the translators have unanimously rendered it "he acquired."

"He created," however, is expressed by a different word among the Hebrews, and that word does not occur in the present passage. And the difference between "he created" and "he acquired" is very great, since "creation," in its more common sense, signifies the passage from non-being into being, while "acquisition" signifies the special belonging of something already existing to the one who acquires it.

So when the Son of God says, "The Lord acquired me the beginning of his ways for his works," he showed at once both his pre-existence and his special belonging to the Father, and at the same time the usefulness and necessity of his own providence and government over his Father's works.

That is why he goes on, "Before the age he founded me, in the beginning, before he made the earth, before the springs of water came forth, before the mountains were set in place, and before all the hills he begets me." By all these words he shows the benefit and necessity of his work for all things, teaching, as he had to, that he was, and was before, and existed prior to the whole world and was its leader. For Moses, in his account of the making of the world, made no mention at all of the supramundane and invisible powers, because of the immaturity of those he was instructing; he described the formation of the visible world, and at the beginning mentioned four elements: heaven, earth, abyss, and water. Of two of these he said that they were made by God ("In the beginning," he says, "God made the heaven and the earth"), but he did not likewise mention of the water and the abyss that these too had come into being; he simply said, "and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was moving over the water." So the Son of God, as was necessary, teaches in the passage before us about these too: that they came into being, and that he himself was before all things, and that all things were made through him.

That is why he says, "Before the age he founded me, in the beginning, before he made the earth, and before he made the abysses, before the springs of water came forth." Having mentioned these three, earth, abyss, and water, he adds the fourth at the end, keeping the greater one, heaven, for last. So he continues, "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him."

These things, then, are clearly set forth by divine Scripture, and we have given a brief account of them in summary form. Let us now hear how Marcellus, dragging the meaning down to the ground, insists that all these things were said about the flesh which the Savior assumed. He writes, word for word, as follows:

"This being so, it follows that we should consider with our mind this chapter, spoken in proverbial form: 'The Lord created me the beginning of his ways.' For our Master, God, truly created, having made what was not. For he did not create the flesh, which the Word assumed, as something that existed, but as something that did not exist." And he adds: "Therefore, even though this new mystery appeared in the very last times, since it had for this reason been predestined before this age, the prophet fittingly said, 'Before the age he founded me,' meaning, of course, the flesh."

And again he goes on to say: "Then he says, 'In the beginning, before he made the earth.' What earth is this, if not clearly our flesh, which after the disobedience became earth again? For he says, 'You are earth, and to earth you will return.'" You see how badly he has gone astray, turning aside from the straight road and devising for himself a rough, hard road, one with no way out, as it were.
Look, then, how he forced everything, preferring to bring himself to utter a shameless and impudent statement rather than confess that the Son of God himself is Wisdom.

He refers "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works" to the person of the Savior, admitting that it is he who says these things in Proverbs. These are his very words: "Therefore, fittingly, since the old things had passed away and all things were about to be made new through the newness of our Savior, our Master Christ cried out through the prophet, saying, 'The Lord created me the beginning of his ways.'"

Having said this, he drags the meaning down to the flesh of our Savior, adding next: "For our Master, God, truly created, having made what was not. For he did not create the flesh, which the Word assumed, as something that existed, but as something that did not exist, the beginning of his ways." And this fine fellow does not understand that it is one and the same discourse, and one and the same person, that says "I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling" and "The Lord created me"; so that if one is referred to the flesh, the other must be as well, and it will be Wisdom who says both.

But if, according to Marcellus, it is the flesh that says "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways," then the flesh would be Wisdom, and it will be the flesh that says, "By me kings reign" and "By me great men are made great." And how could the flesh say, "I will remember to recount the things from of old," to which he adds, "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways"? Marcellus also explains what the ways are, saying next: "For this man has become for us who intend to live righteously the way of godliness, the beginning of all the ways that came after these."

And he adds: "He has fittingly called our Master the Savior 'the beginning of ways' for this reason: because he became the beginning also of the other ways which we have had after the first way, meaning the traditions handed down through the holy apostles, who, according to the prophecy, with lofty proclamation preached to us this new mystery." So much for Marcellus.

3. Now if he did not also accept the scripture of Moses and of the prophets after Moses, his interpretation would have some plausible reason behind it. But since he is not one of those who reject the Old Testament, why ever did he call the apostles and their teachings "ways", and pay no attention to the prophets of God, who have written countless things about the ways of God? First of all Moses wrote: "You shall go by the king's highway," and "Behold, I have set before your face the way of life and the way of death."

David likewise says: "The Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly will perish." Jeremiah says: "Stand in the ways and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord, and see which is the good way, and walk in it." And you will find that each of the prophets mentions the ways of God in various ways.

Our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, teaches that he himself is the beginning of the ways of God when he says, "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works." He was surely older than Moses and the prophets, and older still than those who lived even earlier according to the ways of God. But the flesh he assumed did not come before all of these. So the saying has not been rightly taken to refer to the flesh.
So the Savior did not say these things because of the flesh. He said them because he pre-existed and leads the way on all the ways of God, which all the God-loving men of old have travelled.

The divine apostle says, "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!" In saying this he suggests certain other ways: the ways of providence over the universe, by which God governs all things with divine power, by an ineffable judgment and by reasons beyond our grasp. It follows that the one who said "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works" must be called the beginning of these ways as well. But this man did not understand the ways of God, and declared that our Savior's flesh was their beginning.

He also interprets "for his works", saying: "'He created me,' then, he says, 'as the beginning of his ways, for his works.' And what works does he mean? Those of which the Savior says, 'My Father is working until now, and I am working,' and again, 'I have finished the work,' he says, 'which you have given me.'"

Then, as if clarifying the sense of what had been said, he adds: "For who, before the facts were demonstrated, would have believed that the Word of God, born through a virgin, would take on our flesh and display the whole Godhead bodily in it?" And as if he had now given the complete sense, he concludes: "This, then, is what 'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works' means."

He wrote these things because he could not lift the eyes of his mind on high and say, as the prophet did, "I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you have founded." Nor did he remember the prophetic word which says, "But they do not look upon the works of the Lord, and they do not consider the works of his hands."

Had he paid attention to these things, he would have known that the one who says these things existed, and existed beforehand, before heaven and earth and the whole world. He existed not only before God's visible works but also before his intelligible works, which subsist in incorporeal and supramundane powers. But when he passes on to "Before the age he founded me," he again brings the flesh into the middle. He speaks as follows, calling this a foundation: "his economy according to the flesh, which was foreordained."

"As the apostle also says, 'For no one can lay any other foundation than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.'" And he adds: "Here he mentions one age, from which he said the things concerning Christ had been founded, even though many ages have passed, as David said: 'He who exists before the ages.'"

Passing next to "In the beginning, before he made the earth," he again says that the earth is the flesh. He writes as follows: "What is this earth, if not plainly our flesh, which after the disobedience became earth again? For 'You are earth,' he says, 'and to earth you shall return.' This flesh had to be healed." Our most wise friend says this without remembering that a little earlier he had said that the flesh was created as the beginning of God's ways before God made the earth.

But if by "earth" he really meant the flesh, how can one avoid admitting that the one who says he existed before the earth was made pre-existed the flesh? For he says, "Before the age he founded me, in the beginning, before he made the earth." Therefore the one who says this existed before the flesh was made.

Even if he mentioned not many ages but one, the age the Savior also mentioned when he said, "The children of this age marry and are given in marriage," even so it was not the flesh our Savior assumed that existed before the present age. It was he himself, the one who teaches these things through Solomon. You see what a tight spot a man gets into when he turns aside from the straight and royal road.

To what has been said he adds this as well: "'Before he made the abysses,' he says. Here the prophet, speaking in proverbs, says that the abysses are the hearts of the saints, which hold the gift of the Spirit in their depths." He does not understand that the holy prophets of God shared in the same Spirit before our Savior's coming in the flesh: Moses, and those who were older still than Moses. If these abysses really were the hearts of the saints, then the one who says "before he made the abysses" must be older than all of them.

How, then, could these words be referred to the Savior's flesh? Indeed, if he had any knowledge of the divine Scriptures, he would not so readily have declared that the abysses are the hearts of the saints. He would have noticed that, according to the testimony of Moses, "darkness was upon the abyss," and that divine Scripture says much about the abysses that is hard to interpret. The apostle says, "Do not say, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'

(that is, to bring Christ down), or 'Who will descend into the abyss?' (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead)." In these words, at any rate, he seems to have called the regions of Hades "the abyss". The Lord himself made this even clearer in his oracle to Job, when he said: "Have you come to the spring of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the abyss? Are the gates of death opened to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?"

Then there are the evil powers in the abyss, of which it is said, "Praise him from the earth, you dragons and all abysses," and the darkness upon the abyss, of which Moses said, "and darkness was upon the abyss." If he had read the divine Scriptures with diligence rather than superficially, he would have learned all this, and he would not have dared to call the abysses the hearts of the saints.

He would also have known in what sense it is said, "Abyss calls to abyss at the sound of your cataracts," and again, "The abysses were troubled, a multitude of the sound of waters," and again, "The abyss is his covering, like a garment."

He would have examined these passages and others like them closely, if he had cared at all to understand them. As it is, he declared so offhandedly and loosely that the abysses are the hearts of the saints. Even so, he did not understand that the one who said "before he made the abysses" was teaching that he existed before the holy and God-loving men who have lived from the beginning of time. So from every side it is clear that the words in question cannot be fitted to the Savior's flesh.

Moving on to another saying of the same Scripture, he interprets it too, saying: "What, then, is this heading as well: 'before the springs of the waters came forth'?" He says they are the holy apostles. "This mystery is presented to us by the scripture of Exodus, which long ago foretold the types of the apostles.

Since the apostles were twelve in number, it mentions twelve springs." In saying this he does not understand that Israel too had twelve tribes and twelve patriarchs of those tribes, and that the Twelve Prophets form a single book. There are also twelve hours in the day and twelve months in the whole year.

Why, then, should the number twelve belong to the apostles more than to all of these, if a mere count was what gave him grounds for interpreting the passage this way? He ought to have seen that the prophets of God were not strangers to the springs either, since they shared in the same Holy Spirit. That is why it is said of them in the Psalms, "In the assemblies bless God the Lord, from the springs of Israel."

So one must also confess that the Son of God, who says "before the springs of the waters came forth," existed before those springs too. But listen to how he interprets it. He says: "Fittingly, then, the Master spoke through the prophet Solomon about his birth according to the flesh when he said, 'before the springs of the waters came forth.'"

And he adds: "For this is what the Savior said to the holy springs: 'Go and make disciples of all nations.'" Then, as if summing up his argument, he draws the conclusion of his exposition: "From every side it is clear that the prophet also called the holy apostles 'springs' figuratively." So he wants the apostles to be the springs, but the prophets do not satisfy him.

Why not? Is it not because he could not place the Savior's flesh before them? Yet the Son of God, who teaches these things about himself in Proverbs, existed even before the natural, perceptible springs. Moses mentioned these in his account of creation, saying, "A spring went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth," and again, "A river goes out from Eden to water the paradise." And the one who gave the oracle to Job also mentions springs of the sea, saying, "Have you come to the spring of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the abyss?"

Scripture also teaches that there are certain waters above the heavens, when it says, "Praise him, you heavens of heavens, and the waters above the heavens." It follows that we should think of those waters too, whatever their nature may be, as having springs of some kind. Then the one who said that he pre-existed "before the springs of the waters came forth" would be shown to be older than those as well.

But he gives no thought to any of this and is unwilling to make the effort. He keeps to the same line, since he also says this: "'Before the mountains were settled,' he says, 'and before all the hills he begets me.' By mountains and hills he means the apostles and the successors of the apostles. Speaking in proverbs, he indicates their righteous way of life compared with that of other people."

So the same people were the springs, the same the mountains, and the same the hills! With visible springs and mountains it would be against nature to say they are the same thing, for in terms of quality springs of water have nothing in common with the heights of mountains. In the same way, when things are contemplated allegorically in the mind, one must show a difference between the springs, the mountains and the hills understood in that contemplation. But he knows nothing that has been carefully tested, and he confuses everything through carelessness. He has declared that the same people are springs of water and mountains and hills, and says that all of these are the apostles, without distinguishing how they differ.

Why, then, did he not likewise call those who were perfected in righteousness and piety before our Savior's flesh "mountains" and "hills"? Was it not because he could not make the Savior's flesh exist before them? So referring these words to the Savior's flesh is forced and strained. And how could "he begets me" fit the flesh? He said that he was begotten before the springs, before the mountains and before the hills, when he said, "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works; before the age he founded me."

If, then, the flesh says these things, as Marcellus thinks, how could the flesh say, "and before all the hills he begets me"? Suppose the flesh did come before the apostles. How then does it say that it was itself begotten by God? For Marcellus seemed to say that the flesh, which did not exist before, was created.

He said: "He truly created, since our Master God made what did not exist. For the flesh which the Word assumed was not something already existing; he created it when it did not exist." We have understood, then, that it was created. But how could one explain its also being begotten by God? Our Savior says, "What is born of the flesh is flesh," and the apostle says, "born of a woman, born under the law."

How, then, could the flesh have said of the God of the universe, "and before all the hills he begets me"? I think it is plain to everyone that this interpretation is forced. Without any forcing, though, and apart from any allegorical method, one could say that these words hold true of the Son of God. He existed before the earth. He was, and existed beforehand, before the bodily springs of the waters came forth, before the abysses in the perceptible sense, and before the shape of the earth was formed with its heights of mountains and hills. For "all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being."

Someone might ask why he did not teach that he existed before the heavens, or before the things in the heavens, or the divine and supramundane powers and spirits beyond them. The answer will be that the passage did not yet mention these, because through Proverbs it was giving a kind of elementary instruction to those whose souls were still infants.

This is clear from what it says. At one point it says, "Hear, son, your father's instruction, and do not reject your mother's rules"; at another, "Son, attend to my laws, and incline your ear to my words"; and again, "Son, do not make light of the Lord's discipline, and do not lose heart when he reproves you"; and "Son,

if you are good to yourself, you will be good to your neighbors too; but if you turn out bad, you alone will bear the evils." You could gather countless similar passages from the book of Proverbs for yourself, and they show that the discourse is addressing those whose souls are still infants.

So too Moses, who was a tutor of those whose minds were immature, mentioned heaven and earth and the creation of visible things. But he did not mention the creation of angels, or of divine powers, or of holy spirits, because his disciples could not yet take in teaching about these.

Fittingly, then, the discourse in Proverbs also drew its teaching for such people from the mountains, hills and springs on earth, as from more familiar things. Starting from a foundation, it meant to lead its pupils by the hand to higher things and to prepare them to pass from lesser things to more divine ones.

So much, then, if one does not inquire beyond the letter. But if someone wishes to understand these things at a deeper level, he will apply them to all the righteous and God-loving men who have ever lived, not to the apostles more than to them. From there he will go on to the divine and angelic powers. He will say that the mountains and hills hint at the different ranks of angels and archangels and divine spirits: thrones and dominions, principalities and authorities.

For the divine apostle taught that all these too were created "through him and for him," and that he is "before all things." He probably took his starting point from here, because in these words the Son of God speaks in his own person: "Before the mountains were settled, and before all the hills he begets me." He said that the other things were settled, but that he alone was begotten before the things mentioned were formed.

The same apostle knows of the heavenly Jerusalem, and of the heavenly mountain on which he says it stands: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven." So the only-begotten Son of God, who pre-existed all these as well, was hinting covertly through Proverbs at the mystery of his own ineffable generation.

That he meant us to understand these things becomes clear from what he adds next: "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him." At this point our noble interpreter of the Scriptures was shut in and came to a halt. He went no further, because he could not make the sequence fit the hypothesis he had put forward about the Savior's flesh.

He had talked about the flesh up and down and declared that everything was said about the flesh. He got as far as the mountains and hills, saying that these were the apostles. But what comes after these he deliberately passed over in silence, and no longer dared to go any further in the Scripture.

Here, then, he halts his discussion. But after a great many things said in between, he abandons the interpretation that refers to the flesh and admits that the one who said these things is the Word of God. These are his very words: "For before the world existed, the Word was in the Father. But when God Almighty resolved to make all things in heaven and on earth, the coming into being of the world required active energy. For this reason, since nothing else existed except God (for it is agreed that all things were made by him), the Word then came forth and became the maker of the world. Even before this he had been preparing it inwardly in thought, as the prophet Solomon teaches us when he says, 'When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him,' and 'when he was making secure the springs of what is under heaven, when he was making strong the foundations of the earth, I was beside him, fitting things together;

I was the one in whom he delighted.' For the Father naturally rejoiced as he made all things through the Word with wisdom and power." So says Marcellus. If, then, he finally and reluctantly admitted that these things were said in the person of the Word, he must accept that the whole connected passage refers to that same Word of God.

The one who said "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him" is the same one who said "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works." At the outset we showed that a single person speaks throughout the passage. So the very one who said "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works" went on to add "Before the age he founded me," and "In the beginning, before he made the earth," and "Before the mountains were settled, and before all the hills he begets me."

The same one also added "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him" and what follows. If, then, the Word was the one who said these things, how could he be inside God, unbegotten together with God and one and the same with him, and still say that he was created and begotten? For, as I said, it was shown that one and the same person speaks throughout the passage.

If he admitted, however belatedly, that these words were spoken in the person of the Word who is in God, then his application of them to the Savior's flesh was forced, and all those arguments of his together have been exposed as stale, empty and superfluous. Suppose instead, according to the interpretation he gave, that it was the Savior's flesh that said "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works." Suppose the flesh was founded before the age, and in the beginning, before he made the earth (the earth being, of course, the flesh, as he thought, because it is said, "You are earth, and to earth you shall return"). Suppose it was the flesh that said "Before he made the abysses, before the springs of the waters came forth, before the mountains were settled, and before all the hills he begets me" (because, in our most wise friend's opinion, it was begotten before the apostles were chosen). Then it follows that "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him" is also spoken in the person of the flesh.
But no one who was not out of his mind would ever agree to this interpretation. The word of truth will raise a great shout against him and show who it was that spoke throughout this passage.

It was another, the only-begotten Son begotten from God, living and subsisting, who existed even before all things that have come into being were formed. He himself shows this here by what he adds next: "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him." For he was with God and present with him before the heaven came into being, along with what lies beyond heaven and everything in heaven. This, at any rate, is what he hinted at by saying, "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him."

And how did God prepare it, if not by laying down and designing, before it came into being, the way in which it was to be formed? The Father, then, designed and prepared it. He considered how so great a heaven should be formed: what size and what shape it required, and how many measures and parts, for the sake of the things that would be contained within it, the things that would be outside it, and those that would run their courses in it. The Son, meanwhile, gazed intently on the Father's thoughts, and he alone beheld the depths within him. He went to work, carrying out the Father's commands.
That is why it is said somewhere: "Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the heights.

Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all you stars and light. Praise him, you heavens of heavens, and the waters above the heavens. Let them praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke and they came into being, he commanded and they were created."

But even before the heaven itself came into being, along with what lies beyond heaven and everything in heaven (one word has been used to stand for all of them), the Son of God existed. He was present with the Father and beside him while the Father was still deliberating about how all these things were to be formed. That is why he says, "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him." Then, like a good painter, he took the archetypal forms from the Father's thoughts and transferred them to the substances of the works. He gave life and existence to things exactly as he saw them already present in the Father's mind.

He himself would be a trustworthy witness to these things, for he teaches as follows in the Gospels: "Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing something; for whatever he does, the Son does likewise.

For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing." Here one might reasonably ask how the Son does once again the things that the Father has already made once. But he himself resolved the question when he said, "For whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise."

So the things the Son does are likenesses of archetypal works that already exist beforehand in the Father's secret thoughts. Gazing intently at these in the Father's mind, the Son made copies of what he saw. And he showed that his beholding of the Father's depths is the work of the Father's love, making this clear in what follows, where he says, "For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself does." So as the Father shows him, the Son contemplates the Father's hidden things and through his works gives existence to the works of the Father's counsel. Being thus with the Father, and present with him as he was preparing the heaven and what is in it, he taught this when he said, "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him."

And the Father rejoiced even before the world came into being, looking upon his own only-begotten Son and seeing himself reflected in him as in an image. That is why Wisdom says, "I was the one in whom he delighted day by day." But the Son too was filled with gladness, rejoicing at the sight of the Father. He himself teaches this when he says, "And I rejoiced before him at every season, when he rejoiced at having completed the world."

Here "the world" is to be understood as the whole completed sum of all created things. As this was brought from nonexistence into being through the Son, the God of all things rejoiced. Such, then, would be the true account, set out briefly and in summary from the divine Scripture. But Marcellus, by carrying the passage down from above to the flesh of our Saviour, has run its meaning aground, twisting and misinterpreting the true sense of the divinely inspired Scripture.
Moreover, turning to the Word, he says that it was the Word that is within the Father, as in his reasoning and thought, that prepared the heaven.

These are his very words: "For before the world was made, the Word was in the Father. But when God the Almighty resolved to make all things in the heavens and on the earth, the coming into being of the world required an active energy. And for this reason, since there was nothing else besides God (for it is agreed that all things were made by him), the Word then came forth and became the maker of the world, the Word who had earlier been preparing it inwardly, in thought, as the prophet Solomon teaches us when he says, 'When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him.'"

Here we should consider how, deliberately playing deaf, he does not hear the words "I was present with," which plainly signify the presence of the Son together with the Father. Instead, contrary to Scripture, he declares that there was no one else besides God before created things came into being. He did not shudder at uttering this statement, which is a denial of the Son, nor was he abashed before the divine Scripture, which testifies that before the creation of heaven the Son alone was present with the Father. For it says, "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him."

The prefix "with," added to "being present," indicates presence at the same time together with another. So he teaches not simply that he was present, but that he was present together with the Father. And the Father too did not simply rejoice, but rejoiced in the presence of the Son. That is why he says, "I was the one in whom he delighted day by day."

And how could rejoicing before the Father suit a Word that has no subsistence of its own, but is in God himself and acts only by way of signifying? For "rejoicing" and "before him" plainly establish his own subsistence. But Marcellus takes no account of any of this. He sets aside the Son, and says instead that the Word, being within God, at one time goes forth by an active energy, and at another time remains within him without acting. And he does not see that to speak of something being inside and outside God presupposes something composite and a bodily condition, which it is not right to admit in the case of the unbegotten and incorporeal nature.

And how did the Word come forth and become the maker of the world? Was it by tongue and voice, or did God presumably use speech of some kind? And with whom could he have conversed, when no one else was with him? To whom could he have spoken, when no one was present? Or did he speak to himself, using voice and speech, so that the Word came forth from him?

And why could he not have established what he willed by an active power while the Word was still within him? After all, among human beings too, most craftsmen complete their works in silence, especially when they work with no one present. What, then, prevented God from establishing all things in some such way, having the Word within himself? Yet Marcellus even offers the image of a sculptor talking to himself and saying to himself, "Come, let us make, come, let us fashion a statue." In the same way, he says, God, the Lord of the universe, also said to himself, "Let us make man," as has already been shown many times in what came before, and by this, I think, his denial of the Son of God has been laid bare.

For to claim that God converses with himself while having his own Word within him would belong to a Jewish way of thinking, while to say that he is himself the Father of the Word within him, and that the Word within him is his Son, was the mark of the heresy of Sabellius.

So too, again, is the claim that the three are one, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; for this also belongs to Sabellius. Marcellus himself declared exactly this, writing somewhat as follows: "For it is impossible for three hypostases, if they exist, to be united in a monad, unless the triad first had its origin from a monad. For the holy Paul said that those things are summed up in a monad which in no way differ from God in unity; for in unity the Word and the Spirit alone differ [?] from God."

Then he tries to establish this, going on next to say: "If, then, the Word is seen to have come forth from the Father himself and to have come to us, while the Holy Spirit, as Asterius too confessed, proceeds from the Father, and again the Savior says of the Spirit, 'He will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and declare it to you,' does not the monad here clearly and plainly appear, by an ineffable account, expanded into a triad, yet in no way submitting to division?

"For if the Word proceeds from the Father, and the Spirit too is confessed to proceed from the Father, and again the Savior says of the Spirit, 'He will take from what is mine and declare it to you,' is it not then plain that some hidden mystery is being unveiled? For how, unless the monad, being indivisible, were expanded into a triad, could he say of the Spirit at one time that he proceeds from the Father, and at another, 'He will take from what is mine and declare it to you,' and again, breathing on the disciples, say, 'Receive the Holy Spirit'?

"For how, if he proceeds from the Father, does he promise that he will receive this ministry from the Son? For if they were two divided persons, as Asterius said, it would necessarily follow either that the Spirit, proceeding from the Father, does not need the ministry of the Son (for whatever proceeds from the Father must be perfect, in no way needing help from another), or, if he receives from the Son and ministers grace from the Son's power, that he no longer proceeds from the Father."

And after other things he adds: "But if the Gospel said that, breathing on the disciples, he said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' it is clear that the Spirit came forth from the Word. How then, if the Spirit came forth from the Word, does the same Spirit again proceed from the Father?" And after other things he adds: "So he did not speak rightly or fittingly in saying that there are three hypostases, and he said it not once but a second time." By these arguments and others like them this most wise man tries to establish that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one and the same, three names being applied to one hypostasis.

For even in these matters he did not understand how the Son is said to proceed from the Father and the Holy Spirit likewise, nor was he able to grasp how the Savior said of the Holy Spirit, "He will take from what is mine and declare it to you," nor how, breathing on his disciples, he said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." For those who consider it piously, this will be easily resolved, if one reckons that the Son, always being with the Father and present to him, was somewhere within, as it were in the inaccessible and untrodden sanctuaries of the Father's kingdom, and then, being sent out by the Father for the salvation of the human race, said that he had come out from the Father. This he also showed elsewhere about himself through a parable, saying, "The sower went out to sow."

For from where did he go out, if not from the innermost palaces of the Father's Godhead? By the same reasoning the Holy Spirit too, which always stands beside the throne of God (since "ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him," according to Daniel), was itself also sent, at one time in the form of a dove upon the Son of Man, at other times upon each of the prophets and apostles.

That is why it too is said to proceed from the Father. And why are you surprised? Even of the devil it has been said, "And the devil went out from the Lord," and a second time again, "And the devil went out from the presence of the Lord." You would find the same in the case of Ahab too, where Scripture says, "And an evil spirit came out and stood before the Lord and said, 'I will deceive him.'"

But these are opposing spirits, and how and in what sense this was said, now is not the time to inquire. The only-begotten Son of God, however, teaches that he has come out from the Father because he is always with him; and likewise the Holy Spirit, which is something other than the Son. The Savior himself shows this clearly when he says, "He will take from what is mine and declare it to you." For this would be direct proof that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not one and the same; for whatever receives something from another is understood to be other than the one who gives.

And that the Holy Spirit is other than the Son, our Savior and Lord himself taught expressly, in various ways and in the plainest words, when he said to his disciples: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive." You see how he says that the Spirit, the Paraclete, is another, and different from himself. And if, breathing on the disciples, he said, "Receive the Holy Spirit," we must not fail to recognize that the breathing was in some way a purification of the apostles' souls, preparing them to be fit to receive the Holy Spirit.

For he is not said to have breathed into their face, nor to have breathed the breath of life, nor the Holy Spirit, as is written of Adam, that "God breathed into his face the breath of life"; rather, it is said that he first breathed, and then said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." And his giving of the Spirit in turn showed him to be other than what was given.

For the giver and what is given could not be the same. Rather, the one bestowing was the Savior, what was given was the Holy Spirit, those receiving were the apostles, and the breathing was, as I said, a purification of the apostles, or else what brought about the imparting of the Holy Spirit; for it can be understood either way.

In any case, these passages show that the Holy Spirit is other than he, as do the words that follow, where again it is recorded that he said: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him."

To which he adds: "These things I have spoken to you while I remain with you; but the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom my Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and remind you of all that I have said to you." You hear how he used the plural, "we will come and make our dwelling with him," speaking of himself and the Father, and how, when speaking of the Holy Spirit, he spoke as of another, saying, "he will teach you all things."

Of the same kind was the saying, "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth." So the Paraclete, about whom he taught so much, was other than he. Fittingly, then, he added again: "These things I have spoken to you while I remain with you; but the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom my Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and remind you of all that I have said."

"For I," he says, "have spoken these things to you for the present; but the Spirit of truth, whom my Father will also send, will teach you all things, all that you have not learned now because you could not take them in;

"but he, when he comes (I mean the Paraclete), will complete the teaching, as well as bringing to your remembrance what I am now saying." And again he adds: "When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me." By all of these he clearly shows that the one sent by him, who was to bear witness about him, is other than himself.

He develops the point still further in what he adds: "But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you." In speaking here of his going away he signified both his passion and his ascent to the Father after it.

Who, then, is so foolish as to say, after so many statements, that the one who says these things and the one about whom he said them are one and the same, when he hears him plainly declaring that he is telling the truth, and setting out what that truth is: that unless he himself went away, the Holy Spirit would never come?

And if he declares at one time that the Father will send the Holy Spirit and at another that he himself will, he is surely not teaching contradictory things; for "whatever he sees the Father doing," these things the Son also does likewise, and "as he hears, he judges." So by the Father's judgment, and when the Father wills, then the Son, and † through him the Savior [?], sends to his disciples the Spirit of truth, the Paraclete, to comfort and console them for what they suffered from their persecutors while preaching the gospel;

and not only to comfort them, but also to teach them the whole truth of the new covenant, which they were not able to be taught by the Savior when he was speaking these things with them, because they were still enslaved to the Jewish way of life.

He fulfilled these things in deed after his resurrection from the dead. After it, having said to Mary, "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father," he later appeared to the disciples as one who had gone up to the Father, the Holy Spirit having been sent and being with him and standing ready for the ministry to which it had been appointed; and at that time he also allows them to touch him.

For it was then that he breathed on them, and then that he gave them a certain portion of the gift of the Holy Spirit, the portion that brings about the forgiveness of sins. For "there are varieties of gifts," of which he bestowed on them a part at that time, while he was with them and present to them; but afterward he filled them with a greater and more perfect power. Of this he spoke to them in the Acts of the Apostles: "But you will receive power from on high when the Holy Spirit has come upon you." At that time he also promised that they would be baptized in the Holy Spirit, and this too was fulfilled after his ascension, when on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit was sent to them in keeping with his words.

Since the matters in this passage require further elaboration and clarification, this is not the time to go through them with the precision of a full examination, since that is not our present purpose. What needed to be shown was that the Paraclete Spirit is other than the Son, and this has been demonstrated in various ways from what the Savior himself taught, both in other places and where he said: "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will tell you all the truth;

"for he will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and declare it to you." Here again he promises that his disciples will learn from the Holy Spirit what he himself did not teach, speaking as of another when he says "when he comes," and "he will not speak on his own," and "he will glorify me," and "because he will take from what is mine." For to suppose that the Savior says all these things about himself is a dreadful and almost incurable simplemindedness.

No, through these words the Savior himself clearly taught that the Holy Spirit exists as other than himself: surpassing in honor and glory and rank, and better and higher than every intellectual and rational being (which is why it has also been included with the holy and thrice-blessed Triad),

yet subordinate to him. He showed this when he said, "For he will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will speak." And from whom he will hear, he makes plain by saying, "He will take from what is mine and declare it to you"; from my treasure, that is, for "in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge."

He himself, then, as the only-begotten Son, receives from the Father and hears from the Father, while the Holy Spirit is supplied by him. That is why he says, "He will take from what is mine and declare it to you." Now, the God who is over all is also called spirit, as the Savior himself taught when he said, "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth"; and he himself would truly be the Holy of holies, and the one "who rests among the holy." But the Son of God too is spirit, and he too is a spirit, holy of holies, if indeed he is the image of the invisible God.
That is why it is said of him as well, "Now the Lord is the Spirit," and "A spirit before our face, Christ the Lord."

But since the Holy Spirit is other than the Father and the Son, the Savior, to show its distinctive property, called it the Paraclete, using the title "Paraclete" to set it apart from others who share the common name, since the angelic powers too would be spirits; for it is said, "who makes his angels spirits." Yet none of these can be made equal to the Paraclete Spirit. That is why it alone has been included with the holy and thrice-blessed Triad,

since the Savior commanded his apostles to hand on the mystery of his rebirth to all from the nations who believe in him in no other way than by "baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." The Father bestows the grace with sovereign authority; the Son ministers it (for "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ"); and the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, is itself what is supplied, according to the varieties of gifts within it: "for to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit," and likewise the rest listed with these.

6 The Holy Spirit, then, by its nature delights to dwell in the holy alone, being supplied through the Son to those whom the Father judges fit. And this would be its work: to sanctify all those to whom it imparts one or more of the gifts within it, so that prophets and apostles and every God-loving soul, and probably the higher and divine powers as well, share in the holiness that comes from it. But the Son alone, honored with the Father's Godhead, would be the maker and creator of all things that have come into being, visible and invisible, including the very existence of the Paraclete Spirit; for "all things came into being through him,

and without him not one thing came into being," and "in him all things were created, those in the heavens and those on earth, whether visible or invisible." But the God who is beyond all things, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, being an ineffable good, surpassing all reasoning and thought, every word and conception, the head at once of all things whatever and of whatever kind they are, of the Holy Spirit itself, and moreover of the only-begotten Son, is fittingly the only one proclaimed by the apostle as God "over all and through all and in all," when he says: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all."

And he alone may be styled the one God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, while the Son is "the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father." But the Paraclete Spirit is neither God nor Son, since it has not received its origin from the Father in the same way as the Son; it is one of the things that came into being through the Son, since "all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being."

These mysteries, then, are handed down to the holy catholic Church in some such way through the divine utterances. But Marcellus, mixing everything together, at one time plunges into the whole abyss of Sabellius, at another tries to revive the heresy of Paul of Samosata, and at another is plainly convicted of being a Jew. For he introduces one hypostasis with three faces, as it were, and three names, saying that God and the Word in him and the Holy Spirit are the same.

Then, moving on from here to the apostle's teachings on the divinity of Christ, he again resorts to perverse interpretations. For when the divine apostle expressly speaks of the Son of God as God, saying, "who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, for in him all things were created, those in the heavens and those on earth, whether visible or invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities; all things were created through him and for him; and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together,"

7 this marvelous man, falling back once more onto the flesh, declares that the flesh is the image of the invisible God, not hearing that "who is the image" is expressed in the masculine form. For applying "who" to the flesh, I know not how, he said that it is the flesh that is meant, as though the flesh itself were "the image of the invisible God." And again he says that "he is before all things" was said of the flesh, not ashamed to take "he" as referring to the flesh.

He also says that he was called "the firstborn of all creation" on account of the flesh, and he persists unabashed in claiming that "the things in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible" were created in the flesh. Nor is he ashamed to say that thrones and dominions and rulers and authorities were counted worthy of the creation in Christ through the Savior's flesh. But since I have already set out Marcellus's words on these matters in my previous work, I will keep my discourse within bounds and be content with their testimony. And I do not think it necessary to argue further that such an exposition of the apostle's words is perverse and forced, since the shamelessness of the interpretation is obvious to anyone.

Yet after saying so much about the Savior's flesh, he does not keep even the flesh safe for us; if only he had at least kept a pious view regarding it! As it is, after all he has said about it, he declares that at the consummation of the ages it is left bereft of the Word, writing as follows: "If, then, he confesses that the flesh profits him nothing, how is it possible that what is from the earth and profits nothing should be with the Word in the ages to come as though it were of use to him?"
