And he repeats the same thing in another place, saying: "If, then, Paul said that at the time of the restoration of all things even creation itself will be changed from slavery to freedom (for he says, 'creation itself will be set free from its slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God'), how could the form of the slave that the Word assumed, being the form of a slave, still be with the Word on account of it [?]?"

You see what sort of words he has dared to utter against the flesh of our Saviour. He did not notice that even before the ascension into heaven, while it was still on earth and before the passion, the Saviour glorified it like this on the mountain. To his three chosen disciples alone he showed an image of his kingdom, so that his face flashed like lightning and gleams of light shone out

(for the divine Scripture says, "His face became like the sun, and his garments white as the light"). Nor did he understand what sort of "body of glory" of Christ the divine apostle was speaking of, and how he taught that our bodies too would be conformed to that body, when he said, "who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory." Nor did he grasp in what way the mortal would be swallowed up by life, as the apostle wrote: "because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life." Ignorant of these things, he asserts that the Word will become one and the same with God, just as he was before, while the flesh, abandoned by the Word, will become I know not what.

Listen, then, to how he puts it: "But if someone should ask about this flesh which became immortal in the Word, what do we say to him? That we do not consider it safe to lay down doctrine about things we have not learned precisely from the divine Scriptures. For how could those who overturn the doctrines of others do such a thing?

But to those who wish to learn from us the precise account of this matter we shall say that, obeying the holy apostle, we know that it is fitting for us to see the hidden mysteries in the way he himself said: 'For now we see,' he says, 'through a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face,' and so on. So do not ask me about things I have not clearly learned from the divine Scripture. For this reason, then, I shall not be able to speak clearly about that divine [?] flesh which shared in the Word." And so he who admits that he can say nothing, and that he has learned nothing from Scripture,

has made such pronouncements about the flesh. He neither took them from Scripture, nor received them from others, nor learned them from the Church, but fashioned them for himself and devised from his own imagination an offspring foreign and alien to the truth. He did not even call to mind the Scripture that says, "Do not add to his words, lest he reprove you and you be found a liar," and "Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart."

See, then, into what great impiety he has fallen. He brought down the whole theology of the pre-existent only-begotten Son to the flesh, and in so many words proclaimed it a crown of victory (for this is what he said: that the Word of God had caused the human flesh to become immortal through the resurrection, and sits at the right hand of the Father as though he had bound on a crown of victory). Yet this same man says that the flesh will be left deserted and orphaned at the end of all things. He unites the Word with God but separates the flesh from the Word's activity, and leaves it, I know not how, immortal and incorruptible, yet lifeless and no longer moved by the Word.

And again he tries to establish these things from the divine readings, which he has not understood. For our Saviour said to those who did not understand his teaching about his flesh and blood: "Does this offend you? Then what if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and are life."

Without attending to the sense of the saying, Marcellus supposed that the Saviour was setting aside the flesh which he had taken from the holy Virgin. Then from this he tries to establish that after the consummation of all things the Word in God will leave the flesh bereft of his own activity. At any rate, he says in these very words: "For concerning the flesh which he had when he conversed with the disciples, he speaks thus: 'Does this offend you? Then what if you see the Son of Man going away to where he was before? The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing.' If, then, he admits that the flesh profits him nothing, how can that which is from the earth and profits nothing be with the Word in the ages to come, as though it were of use to him?" You see how he has distorted the Gospel saying, because he did not understand the saving utterance of the Word: how it was spoken and for what reason.

But you, take up the Gospel scripture and look at the whole teaching of our Saviour, and see how he was speaking not about the flesh he had assumed but about his mystical body and blood. He had fed the crowds with the five loaves and shown this great miracle to those who saw it. But most of the Jews made light of what had happened and said to him, "What sign, then, do you do, that we may see and believe?" Then they brought up the manna in the wilderness, saying, "Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat."

To this the Saviour answered, "Truly, truly I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven." Then he adds, "I am the bread of life," and again, "I am the bread that came down from heaven," and again, "And the bread that I will give is my body." And once more he adds, "Truly, truly I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves.
Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.

Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him." As he set out these and similar things in a rather mystical way, some of his disciples said, "This saying is hard; who can listen to it?" The Saviour answered them, saying, "Does this offend you? Then what if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?

It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and are life." By these words he was teaching them to hear in a spiritual sense what had been said about his flesh and blood. "Do not think," he says, "that I am speaking of the flesh I wear, as though you had to eat it, and do not suppose that I am commanding you to drink perceptible, bodily blood. Know well that the words I have spoken to you are spirit and are life." So the words and sayings themselves are the flesh and the blood. Whoever continually partakes of them is nourished as if with bread from heaven and will share in heavenly life.

"So do not let this offend you," he says, "what I have said about eating my flesh and drinking my blood. And do not be disturbed by a superficial hearing of what I have said about flesh and blood. These things profit nothing when heard in a bodily sense; it is the Spirit that gives life to those who are able to hear spiritually."

But the new interpreter of the Gospel teachings understood none of this. Listen to how he writes, in these very syllables: "Touching his human body and showing it to those who were looking on, he said, 'Does this offend you? Then what if you see the Son of Man going up to where he was before? The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing.'"

One might say to him: Where did you get this addition, my fine fellow, of things not found in the Gospel scripture? That the Saviour touched his human body, showed it to those looking on, and said, "Does this offend you?" is your own invention, and you dare to make the addition on your own authority. Taking this bold invention from himself, he thinks he can establish from it that the Saviour's flesh will be left bereft of the Word's activity, saying: "If, then, he admits that the flesh profits him nothing, how can that which is from the earth and profits nothing be with the Word in the ages to come, as though it were of use to him?" So ignorantly and unskilfully did he set about misinterpreting the Gospel saying. And he likewise gave distorted interpretations of the apostle's words too.

For instance, in the Acts of the Apostles, Peter said of our Saviour, "whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration." Not understanding the sense of the saying, Marcellus tries to use it to put a limit on the kingdom of Christ. He claims that some boundary and fixed term for his kingdom is indicated by the words "until the times of restoration."

He says that this same point is also established by the Psalm that says, "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet," and that this is why the apostle Paul said, "For he must reign until he has put the enemies under his feet." For he supposed that "until" and "as far as" signify a limited time. Listen, then, to how he writes, word for word: "For this reason, it seems to me, God the Almighty, the Master, says to him, 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.' Seeming to separate him by activity alone, because of the human flesh, and as it were setting him a definite time for sitting at his right hand, he says to him, 'until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.'

The holy apostle, interpreting this prophetic saying of David more clearly for us, put it something like this: 'For he must reign until he makes his enemies a footstool for his feet.' Therefore his economy and kingdom as man appear to have a limit." And after other remarks he adds: "And this is why the Acts of the Apostles teach thus about this man whom the Word of God assumed, and, having assumed him, sits at the right hand of the Father: 'whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration.' They too, as it were, fix a boundary and a set term."

To this, after other remarks, he adds: "How, then, could the form of the servant which the Word assumed, being the form of a servant, still be with the Word through him? At any rate, the divine Paul has said clearly and expressly that the Word's economy in the flesh, which came about for our sake, took place within a short span of time out of the past and future ages, and that, just as it had a beginning, so it also has an end. He puts it like this: 'Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father.'"

With all these words Marcellus has failed to recognize the Son's "body of glory" and denies his endless kingdom. He did not notice that "until" is regularly used according to a usage peculiar to Scripture. Thus the Saviour said to the disciples, "Behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age." He was not denying that he would be with them after the consummation as well. He was teaching that for now he would be with them until the consummation, watching over and guarding all who are his disciples, and that after the consummation he would be with them in a better way, making them sharers in his kingdom.

In the same way, then, "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet" and "whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration" were not said as though he would no longer be there afterwards. They were said because at the time of the consummation he is to rise from his Father's throne and make a second descent from heaven, about which the apostle teaches, saying: "For the Lord himself, with a command, with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord." The Saviour, therefore, must remain in heaven and sit at the right hand of the Father "until the consummation." But at the very consummation of all things he will make his glorious second coming and take his saints to himself, so that they may be with him always, not for a limited time but for an endless age. "And so," he says, "we shall always be with the Lord."

So the saints, who will always be with him, will enjoy his kingdom in the kingdom of heaven that has been proclaimed. But our fine fellow did not understand this. The divine apostle said of our Saviour, "For he must reign until he has put the enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death," and again, "And when all things are subjected to him,

then he himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all." Following his usual habit, Marcellus misinterprets these words too, taking "the Son will be subjected to the Father", I know not how, to mean "the Word will be united with God." Yet when was he not united with him, if indeed he was the Word existing eternally in God? How then does the apostle say, "then he will be subjected to God and the Father"?

We must take note that the apostle said that all things will be subjected to the Son himself, and that he teaches that the Son too will be subjected to the Father with the same subjection, when he says, "And when all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him,

that God may be all in all." Marcellus does not listen. For the apostle does not say that God will be "all" in the Son, but "in all." That would have seemed, if anything, to signify a conjunction and union of all things, if God is to be all things in all. But Marcellus interprets the subjection of the Son as the union of the Word, who will become one and the same with the Father as he was before, as he himself said.

If, then, he defines the subjection to the Father as union, it would follow that the subjection of all things to the Son signifies the same kind of union with him. In that case the Son would no longer exist in his own right, nor would the multitudes of the saved who are to be subjected to him live their own life. Instead there would be a kind of fusion and confusion of the whole universe, with the Son and all the rest becoming one and the same, and not only with one another but with God himself as well.
For if all things are united to the Son, and the Son to the Father, by being subjected, see what follows from his argument.

But when the apostle said that all things will be subjected to the Son, he did not mean union. He meant the obedience that comes from free choice, and the glory and honour that all things will render to him as Saviour and King of the universe. In the same way, the Son's being subjected to the Father would mean nothing other than the glory, honour, reverence and majesty, and the freely chosen obedience, which he too will render "to God and the Father" once he has made everyone worthy of the Father's divinity.

For the present, since they are not yet worthy of it, he himself goes ahead of them as the common Saviour of all and reigns over a kingdom that corrects the imperfect and heals those in need of healing, bringing the enemies of the kingdom under his feet. This is what the Psalm sets forth when it says, "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet."

But he will put the enemies under his feet and establish those worthy of his kingdom in endless life. Then death, the enemy of all, will be abolished last of all. For no one will die any longer, since those worthy of the kingdom will then be living eternal life, and death will naturally fall idle, having no one left to kill.

When things have been arranged in this way, all the saints will be subjected to the Son of God with a saving subjection. Since he is life, they will live eternally; since he is wisdom, they will become wise; since he is the Word, they will be made rational. So too they will become christs, anointed with the Spirit of his fragrance. They will be revealed as luminaries of the new age, supplied with light from him. They will be sons of God, adorned with the Spirit of adoption. And those who are subjected to him will share in the other powers that are in him, so that they become righteous from his righteousness and holy from his holiness. And since "the Word was God," he will not begrudge them even divinity.

In this way the apostle's prophecy will prove true, when he foretold that the saints would become "heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ." Yes, and they will also have heavenly bodies like the sun, moon and stars, and in this too they will share in his glory.

The same apostle showed this when he said, "from which we also await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, by the working of the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself." You see how, by his power to subject all things to himself, he will also transform our body, so as to make ours too "conformed to the body of his glory."

But if our body will be "conformed to the body of his glory," how much more will the body of his own glory share in his kingdom? And if ours will be swallowed up by life, as the apostle testified when he said, "because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life," how much more will his own body, which served his divinity, be swallowed up, not by life alone as ours will be, but also by his divinity? So let no one ask questions or puzzle over what we ought to think about the Saviour's body, when they hear Paul say plainly that "what is mortal" must "be swallowed up by life," and that our body will be conformed to the body of Christ's glory "by the working of the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself."

So then, he will subject all things to himself. And we must understand the saving subjection to be something of this kind, in which "the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him." He will render an indescribable and ineffable subjection fitting for him alone. Gathering around himself, like a choir, all who are under him, he will lead them to God and the Father and offer him the glory, the honour, the reverence and the majesty, since the Father is the cause of all good things.

16 Then, too, the conclusion of the apostolic teaching will be fulfilled, which says, "that God may be all in all." We can understand this from another promise as well, in which God himself has said, "I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." In the present age, however, the promise comes to pass only partly, and only in a few, those who are worthy, in keeping with the words "we know in part and we prophesy in part." But after the consummation of all things, when the new age has come, he will no longer dwell in only a few. He will dwell in all who are then worthy of the kingdom of heaven.

This, then, is how he will be "all in all": by dwelling in them and walking among them, by not disdaining to be their God, and by making all of them his own people. He will be in them as he is also said to be in the Son, as the Son himself teaches when he says, "The Father is in me and I am in the Father." And he will be all things in them by giving himself to all, as far as each one's capacity allows them to share in his Godhead. The thrice-blessed hope and the endless, incorruptible life will be established in this end. Then God will be all in all, filling everyone with the radiance of his Godhead's ineffable light. The Son, exulting and rejoicing in what he has achieved, will set around himself like a crown those whom he has made worthy of blessedness, and he will continue his ageless and endless reign under the Father's oversight. At that time the oracles concerning him will be fulfilled, the others and above all the words the angel Gabriel spoke to the all-holy Virgin about the child to be born of her: that "he will reign forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end."

Reigning then, the Son of God will deliver all those who are ruled under him to his Father. He will not cease to be king or withdraw from his kingship. The divine apostle did not say that he would cease to reign; otherwise he would have written the opposite of what Gabriel declared to the Virgin, that he would reign forever and that of his kingdom there would be no end. He said instead that he would "deliver the kingdom," that is, those ruled under him, "to God the Father."

For when he has brought all to perfection under himself, he will deliver them to the Father, made radiant, as it were, by his achievement, like a deposit he had received. He himself teaches this when he says, "All things have been delivered to me by my Father." So, like a good guardian, he will bring the deposit back safe and sound in every respect and deliver it to God. Like a high priest, he will present to him all who have been made priests under him, clothed in white and gleaming, as if in the most brilliant robes, in the incorruptible bodies of the resurrection. In this way they will not only enjoy the kingdom under him but also be filled with the Father's ineffable good things.

For this is how, according to the apostle, God will be "all in all": the Son will bring those he rules to him, so that the whole may be accomplished, I mean, that the Father may be all in all. As he was formerly in the Son, according to the words "The Father is in me and I am in the Father," so he will then also be in all who have been perfected under the Son.

The apostle did not say that the Son would cease to reign and that God would reign instead. He said that the Son would deliver the kingdom to God the Father, showing the deposit to be safe and fit for the worship and priesthood of the Father, and that God would be all in all, as God dwelling and walking among them and becoming all things to them. To some he will be Master, to others King, to others something else; but to all of them together he will be God, becoming all things to them through the divine virtues and powers that are in him.

This is the end of the thrice-blessed hope that the great apostle sketched when he said, "that God may be all in all." In all of them he will be all things in proportion to each one's capacity, supplying to all the various aspects of his Godhead. But for his only-begotten Son alone he will reserve the exceptional, paternal glory, honor and kingship, which no one else shares.

17 If these things need to be sealed with a prophetic seal, then to make what has been said firm and certain I will call as witness the prophetic Spirit. Through the prophet Ezekiel the Spirit declares these very things in words like these: "Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I will seek my sheep and look after them. As a shepherd seeks his flock on a day of darkness and cloud, when his sheep have been scattered, so I will seek out my sheep." And after other things: "And I will save my sheep, and they shall no longer be plunder. And I will judge between ram and ram.

And I will raise up over them a shepherd, and he shall shepherd them: my servant David, and he shall be their shepherd. And I the Lord will be their God, and David a ruler in their midst. I the Lord have spoken. And I will make a covenant with David." After other things he repeats the same prophecy, saying: "And I will rescue them from all the iniquities in which they sinned, and I will cleanse them, and they shall be my people, and I will be their God. And my servant David shall be ruler in their midst, and he shall be the shepherd of them all."

And again he adds, "And David my servant shall be their ruler forever." Notice that in all these passages God is said to be neither the shepherd nor the ruler of those who will be counted worthy of the blessed end, but their God. It is David who is prophesied to become the ruler and shepherd of these same people. Here Christ is hinted at under a veil by the name of David, because he was born of David's seed.

This is clear from the fact that David had died before the time when these words were spoken. The prophet Daniel declares these things more clearly still, plainly calling the Christ of God "Son of Man," just as the scripture of the holy Gospels usually calls him. He speaks as follows: "I watched in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven, and he reached the Ancient of Days and was brought before him. And to him were given dominion and honor and kingdom, and all peoples, tribes and tongues shall serve him.

His authority is an everlasting authority that shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed." You see how here too the prophet shows that the incorruptible, ageless and endless kingdom will belong not to the Word in God but to the Son of Man. He clearly teaches that the Son of Man, who received the incorruptible kingdom from the Ancient of Days, that is, from his own Father, is someone other than the Ancient of Days.

But Marcellus asserts that they are one and the same, a single hypostasis underlying two names. He even dares to set limits to Christ's kingdom, and he shamelessly declares that Christ's kingdom will come to an end after the time of the judgment. He writes as follows: "Here the apostle reveals to us a very great mystery, saying that there will be an end of Christ's kingdom;

and the end will come when all things are subjected under his feet." He develops the argument somewhere along these lines: "In our preceding passages we said that our Master Christ had a beginning of his kingdom, and we used proofs from the divine scriptures." And he adds: "In short, one could easily draw on countless passages as testimony to show that the man received a beginning of kingship through the Word.

If, then, he received a beginning of kingship no more than four hundred full years ago, it is not at all strange that the apostle says that he, having obtained this kingdom so short a time ago, will deliver the kingdom to God."

After other things he adds: "What, then, do we learn about the human flesh that the Word assumed for our sake not quite four hundred years ago? Will the Word keep it in the ages to come as well, or only until the time of the judgment?" Such things Marcellus dared to say. But the prophets of God declare that Christ's kingdom is endless and say that after the time of the judgment he will hold the rule of the new age. Notice how the prophet Ezekiel first describes a judgment of God's sheep, and only after their judgment sets David over them as shepherd and declares that he will be their ruler.

Daniel first says: "I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire. A river of fire flowed before him. A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and books were opened." Having first seen these things, he next sees the Son of Man on the clouds of heaven, approaching the Ancient of Days and receiving the incorruptible kingdom. So it is then that he will have a beginning of his reign over those worthy of blessedness, in a different and better way than now.

The Gospel bears witness to this. In it the Savior himself seals the words of the prophets when he gives his disciples his teaching on the consummation, in which he taught as follows: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory. All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats, and he will set the sheep on his right and the goats on his left. Then the King will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.'" Note how this agrees with what is said in the prophecy about the judgment of sheep and rams. Note, too, how the Son of Man is presented as King after the judgment of the sheep, while God is his Father.

He himself taught this when he said, "Then the King will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father.'" This corresponds to the one named David in the prophecy, who the text teaches will be shepherd and ruler of the sheep and will shepherd and rule God's flock under God's oversight.

We must also pay attention to this: what the apostle said in the words "when he has abolished all rule and all authority and power" the prophecy hinted at when it said, "And I will destroy the evil beasts from the land."

What could the beasts that long troubled the sheep be, if not the hostile powers? Once they have been removed, the new and renewed age, cleansed of all evil, will have the Son of Man as its King, or, in the veiled language of the prophecy, David as its shepherd and ruler, because he was born of David's seed. God, however, it is said to have not as shepherd or ruler but as God himself. In a way higher than that of shepherd, ruler or king, and by the majesty of his divine power, he will lead not only the sheep but the shepherd himself. For it says, "My servant David shall be their shepherd, and I the Lord will be their God." He calls David "servant" because of the form of a servant that our Savior and Lord took from David's seed.

This was the thrice-blessed end. When our Savior confirms the promised kingdom of heaven to those worthy of it, the God over all, his Father, the supreme good of all things, will give himself to those ruled under the Son, becoming all in all. Our Savior and Lord himself showed this once more when he offered up to his God and Father the great prayer for his disciples, in which he asks: "that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.

The glory that you have given me I have given to them, so that they may be one as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me.

Father, I want those whom you have given me to be with me where I am, so that they may see the glory that you have given me." This is our Savior's great intercession for us: that we may be with him wherever he is; that we may see his glory; that the Father may love us as he loved him; that the Father may give us too what he gave him, and give us too the glory he gave him. He makes all of us one, so that we are no longer many but all one, united to his Godhead and to the glory of his kingdom. This happens not by a fusion into one essence but by our being perfected in the highest virtue.

He taught this when he said, "that they may be perfected." For when he has made us perfect in wisdom, understanding, righteousness, piety and every virtue, we will be joined to the ineffable light of the Father's Godhead. We will become lights ourselves through our union with him, and we will be made sons of God by sharing in fellowship with his only-begotten Son, partaking of the radiance of his Godhead. 19

In this way all of us will become one with the Father and the Son. Just as he said that he and the Father were one, when he declared, "I and the Father are one," so he prays that all of us, imitating him, may share in the same unity. This does not happen in Marcellus's way, by the Word being united to God and joined to his essence. It happens as the Truth bore witness, when the Savior himself said, "The glory that you gave me I have given to them, so that they may be one as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one." In this way the apostolic saying will then also be fulfilled: "that God may be all in all."

Marcellus and those who Sabellianize in the same way as he does usually rely on three texts when they try to show that the Father and the Son are one. Sometimes they keep repeating, "I and the Father are one"; at other times, "The Father is in me and I am in the Father," and "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." Against "I and the Father are one" we should set the passage quoted above, in which he prays for his disciples that they too may all attain the same union. He says, "that they may be one as we are one:

I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one." Against "The Father is in me and I am in the Father" we will set another saying of his, in which he prayed for them: "As you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be in us; and the glory that you have given me I have given to them." Here he clearly shows that the Father is in him in the same way that he wants him to be in us. It is not that he and the Father are one in a single hypostasis. Rather, the Father has shared his own glory with him, and he in turn, imitating the Father, shares it with those who are his own.

That is why he says, "The glory that you gave me I have given to them, so that they may be one as we are one," and, "As you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be in us." So the Father and the Son are one by sharing in the glory. By giving his disciples a share in that glory, he counted them worthy of the same union.

Again, the Father was in him and he was in the Father in the same way the divine apostle teaches about all who are worthy of the heavenly kingdom, when he says, "Then God will be all in all," and in the same way it was said, "I will dwell in them and walk among them." Again, "in him we live and move and have our being." All these things have been said about us, who subsist in our own individual hypostasis, who live, and who have nothing in common with the Father's Godhead.

Why, then, should it be surprising if similar expressions are used of the Son? They do not abolish his hypostasis or teach that he himself is both Father and Son. They show the special and exceptional honor the Father gives him, and the glory of his only-begotten and divine fellowship with the Father.

In the same way, "whoever has seen" him "has seen the Father," because he alone and no one else is "the image of the invisible God," "the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his hypostasis," and exists "in the form of God," as the apostolic teachings say. Someone who looks at an image of the emperor that closely resembles him takes in the features of his form through the painting and so pictures the emperor. In the same way, or rather in a way beyond all words and all comparison, a person may gaze with a clear mind and with the eyes of a purified soul, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, upon the greatness of the power of the only-begotten Son and Lord. He considers how all the fullness of the Father's Godhead dwells in him, how "all things came into being through him," and how "in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible." He reflects that the Father begot him alone as his only-begotten Son, made like him in every respect. Such a person will in effect see the Father himself through the Son, for the Father is seen by those whose minds are purified, of whom it is said, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

Since we set ourselves the aim of brevity, let this serve as an exercise in summary form. These matters call for a great deal more elaboration, but whoever cares to understand them precisely can apply his mind to the readings from the Gospels and the apostles and gather their full meaning from them at leisure. Countless other things are jumbled together incoherently in Marcellus's treatise. A great many are said contrary to the intent of scripture, and others are forced and keep no consistency. Still, I consider that what we have examined has made the general refutation plain to sound-minded readers, and I will be content with this.
